**LOG — TUESDAY**

0547. Arrived. Outside temperature 4°C, wind negligible. Note for the record that the east door still binds in cold weather and will require attention before it becomes a matter of shouldering. I have raised this in three consecutive quarterly returns. No reply, as is customary. The budget arrived last Thursday, unchanged to the pound.

0600. Counterweight raised in the north stairwell. Twenty-two turns of the crank, which is correct; when it was twenty-three last February I stopped and checked the cable and found it sound, and it has been twenty-two since. Pawl engaged. Listened for the settle. It came at about eight seconds, slightly long but within what I would call ordinary.

0615. Register signed. Only my own line to fill, but I fill it in the same hand I have always used and I do not skip the columns for arrival, department, and purpose of visit. Department: Building. Purpose of visit: Duty.

0620–0705. Rounds, upper floors. Galleries 1 through 6 dry and undisturbed. Gallery 7 has a new crack in the plaster above the blocked window, hairline, about 40cm, running with the old crack rather than across it, which I take as a good sign. Photographed for the file. Dust levels normal. The tarpaulins in Gallery 4 remain as I left them and I did not lift them, in accordance with the standing instruction, which I have never seen but which was explained to me by Ramsden when I began and which I have never had cause to doubt.

0705–0730. Sub-basement 2. Water at the third step, as it has stood for eleven years. I record the level to the nearest centimetre in any case. Something has been in the flour I keep down there for the purpose, and the flour has been walked out in a line towards the west drain, which is what I hoped for. Renewed the flour.

0730. Breakfast, twenty minutes. I ate at the desk in the porter's room because the canteen is cold and because it is easier to keep the kettle in one place.

0755–0830. Attended to the plant room. The large brass and glass apparatus against the south wall — I have always called it the condenser, and I am aware the maker's plate says nothing of the kind, but I have called it the condenser for nineteen years and it answers to it. It ran warm again on the upper coil. I ran it down, let it stand a quarter hour, brought it up slowly. Warm still, but even. So long as it is even I am content. If the day comes that it is not even I do not know who I would telephone.

0830–0900. Performed the sounding. Third landing, north, hand flat on the wall between the two bolt-heads, and struck the tuning fork twice against the rail, and waited the full two minutes each time with the fork held to the plaster. Nothing to report. There has never been anything to report. I do not know what I am listening for and Ramsden did not know either — he told me plainly, which I respected him for — only that it is done at half past eight and it is done with the wall and not with the air, and that the second sounding matters more than the first. I have thought about this. If a thing is worth two minutes of a man's morning for nineteen years then either it is worth nothing at all or it is worth a great deal more than the morning, and I am not qualified to say which, and so I do it.

0900. It would have been my father's birthday. He worked forty-one years in a place he could not describe to me either, and I used to think that was a failure of his, a smallness in him, and I understand now that it was not. He would come home and eat and say the boiler had held. That was the whole of it. The boiler had held. I have been meaning to say, if there is anywhere in this book to say it, that I understand it now, and there is not anywhere, so I am saying it here.

0915–1140. Cards. Worked the F drawer, second tray. Forty-one cards checked against the ledger, three found reversed and turned the right way, one found soft at the corner and copied out fresh, the original retained behind the new card as instructed. The ledger and the cards agreed in every particular. They have agreed in every particular for as long as I have been checking them, and I check them because the day they disagree I want it to be in my hand and dated.

1140–1200. Swept the entrance hall, both flights, and the length of the west corridor as far as the fire door. Left the fire door unlocked. It is always to be left unlocked.

1200. Lunch.

1240–1500. Repainted the standpipe in the yard, one coat, and cleared the gutter above the loading bay, which was full of the same brown matter it is full of every year. A bird went over the yard twice, low, going somewhere with intent, and I stopped for it, and then went on.

1500–1545. Second rounds, ground floor. Nothing.

1545. Counterweight checked. Holding.

1600. Lowered the flag. Locked the east door, which bound.

1605. Log closed. Nothing to report. The building held.

Forty years ago the last man off the rock pulled the door to behind him and did not lock it, because there was nothing left inside that wanted anything from him. The lamp had been converted in March. It turns now on a gearless drive, four flashes every twenty seconds, and it has never once been wrong, and no one has stood on the gallery to be lit by it since the handover. The fog detector decides on fog. The battery bank decides on the battery bank. Gulls have taken the cottage roof apart in a slow, patient, forty-year committee, and the light does not care, and this is the whole point: the keeper was never load-bearing. He was the thing you needed in order to get the light started so that the light could demonstrate it had never needed him. That is what he was for. He was the assumption.

You begin by supposing the number can be written down. Two integers, one over the other, nothing left in common between them, the fraction scrubbed to the bone. You have to suppose it. Nothing happens otherwise; the door stays shut and the rock stays dark. So you suppose it, and then you step back and let the machinery turn, and the machinery does not need you either: square both sides, and p² = 4q², and therefore p is even, and therefore p is twice something, and put that back in and q is even too, and now both of them are even, and you told me at the beginning that nothing was left in common. The light comes round. It comes round onto the one thing in the room that cannot survive being seen, which is the sentence you wrote first. You do not correct it. You do not amend it. You take it out and you leave it out on the rock, and the proof stands there running four flashes every twenty seconds with nobody in it, salt going quietly into the hinges of the door you pulled to, and what is left is a true thing whose only inhabitant walked off it.

The word is *island*. You have used it your whole life. You have used it about this rock. Now look at the s. There is no reason for the s. There has never been a reason for the s; it was put there by men who thought the word had a father it did not have, and you have been saying it without the s for forty years, thirty of them out loud, and the letter has been sitting inside the word the entire time doing nothing, drawing no current, load-bearing on nothing, and the word worked anyway. The word ran itself. And now that you have seen it the word will not close again. It has come apart into i, s, l, and the rest, and each letter is a gull on the roof of the cottage taking the roof apart, and the meaning — the actual meaning, land with water round it, the thing you could have pointed to — has gone off the rock in a boat and left the spelling turning on its gearless drive, four flashes, twenty seconds, no one on the gallery, correct forever, uninhabited.

That is the moment. It is not that the word became wrong. It is that the word was always going to survive your leaving, and you found out by leaving, and you cannot get back in, because the thing you supposed in order to begin was the thing the beam swung round and found and put out onto the rock, and the light is still going, and it is going for nobody, and it is going beautifully.

So the assumption was the one you never wrote down.

**arrunt** — the debt incurred by one household when its works send water onto another's ground. Takes only the verb *to carry*; there is no construction for paying or forgiving it. An *arrunt* may be divided among heirs but not extinguished, and the phrase "carried three courses" is understood as an accusation without further specification.

**belu** — foundation; ground presumed to stay. A loan from the hill towns, retained chiefly for their masonry and their tax-posts. In domestic speech, a child's word for a thing broken in such a way that it can no longer be lifted. In adult speech, applied to orchards.

**eshen-nak** — "which course?" The customary first question between strangers, answered by naming the year's channel at one's birth (*see* **shenmo**). Answers are compared for closeness; two people of one course may not marry. No equivalent question exists for place of birth; attempts to translate the hill-town form produce a phrase meaning roughly "which water were you standing in."

**iyya-shen** — the same water twice. Attested in a children's counting rhyme (final line, unstressed) and in one variant of the drowning-song, where it appears without case-marking, so that it cannot be determined whether the word functions as subject, object, or location. Speakers disagree whether it names an impossibility, a punishment, or the dead water of a cut-off bend. Elders asked directly will generally decline, or say it is a word for singing and not for talking.

**kelvath** — the jointed frame of a house: the pegged members that are numbered, drawn apart, bundled, and carried. Reckoned as a family's whole wealth; walls and roofing are not counted, being cut new each course. Also the spine of a person or a fish. To say a man "has forty *kelvath* and no hands" is to call him rich and unmarriageable.

**morrath** — the reading of silt: the grain, colour, and layering of a deposit, and the bent attitude of drowned grass, from which the coming channel is inferred. A skill, not an office; *morrath* is spoken of as something one has in the thumbs. Wrong *morrath* is not lied *morrath*, and the two are never confused in speech: there is no word for a false reading given in good faith, only for the reader, who is called *slow-thumbed* and is not blamed.

**ondu** — a grave the river has taken. A completion. The named dead are recited as *ondu* with the year of their taking, and the recitation is a boast.

**ondu-thei** — a grave the river has not taken after three courses. The obligation falls on the descendants to carry earth to it each year, uphill, in the sight of others, until the water comes for it. Longest known: eleven courses, in the upstream reach, where the bank was set.

**shenmo** — the channel of the present year; also, without further marking, the present year itself. The past is enumerated in courses, not seasons, and a man's age is properly given as a list.

**thusk** — the setting of stone and staked willow to hold a bank against moving. The noun has no neutral or approving form; the same word is used of eating in front of people who are not eating.

**Thuskerin** — the households of the upstream reach, collectively. The plural suffix *-erin* is used elsewhere only of animals taken in numbers and of floodwater. No singular is formed. Marriages into the *Thuskerin* are recorded in the course-recitations by the phrase "carried away," which is otherwise used of goods lost in transport.

# A BESTIARY OF THE SIX UNNAMED BEASTS

*Compiled from older books, which were compiled from older books, and which agree in all particulars.*

---

## I. Of the SEMIVERBUM, called the Halfword

It is a small beast, grey as the inside of the cheek, and it dwells in the warm hollow behind the upper teeth, where it lies flat and is mistaken for the palate itself.

It feeds only on the openings of things: the first breath of a name, the initial letter, that which the tongue has already committed to and cannot recall. It will not touch a word left unbegun. For this reason the Halfword is never encountered by the silent, and hunters who wish to see it must first go out into company and speak boldly of a man whose name they know as well as their own.

It cannot be taken by pursuit. Those who lunge at it are left holding the shape of it, the number of its syllables, the letter it begins with, and nothing else, and this the beast permits as a cruelty. It is taken only by turning the back and speaking of an unrelated matter, whereupon, some hours later, it will come and lay the word at the foot of the hunter like a cat with a bird.

*Wherefore we learn that the wise man never begins a sentence he has not already finished, and that the fluent are of all men the most honest.*

---

## II. Of the VITRARIUS, called the Glazier

The Glazier is found in rooms long inhabited, and chiefly in that high corner above the door which no broom has visited in years. It is thin, and lies against the wall in the manner of a moth.

Upon every used thing there settles a film, invisible, laid down by the eye passing over it ten thousand times; and it is this film, and no other food, that the Glazier eats. When it has fed, the chair stands in the room like a chair copied out of a book. The window is a window of a house one has never entered. The room is perfectly correct in every measurement and belongs to somebody else. This lasts as long as a held breath, and then the film begins again to settle, and the householder resumes his life without complaint.

To take it, come home after a long journey and stand in the doorway without setting down what you are carrying. It will be there, above your head, quite full.

*Wherefore householders are advised to move house every seven years, for the beast is the true cause of homesickness in those who have never gone away.*

---

## III. Of the ALIENUS, called the Changeling of the Ear

Every man is furnished with two throats. The first is of flesh and known to him. The second is of bone, and carries his voice up through the jaw into the ear directly, warming it as bread is warmed under a cloth; and it is this warmed voice, and only this, that a man means when he says *my voice*.

The Changeling sleeps in the small bones of the ear and does not stir for the whole of a life, provided nothing goes wrong. But if a man's own words should come to him from outside, through the air, uncarried by bone and therefore thin and high and wet and eager and belonging to a stranger who is nevertheless making all of his gestures — then the beast wakes, and bites once, and sleeps again.

It is captured thus: take a starling and teach it, over one winter, a sentence you are accustomed to saying. In spring, stand near the cage and let it speak. The beast will be found at the moment you look away from the bird.

*Wherefore it is plain that the beast is bred by vanity alone, and that the humble man, having no love of himself, may hear his own voice at any hour and take no hurt from it.*

---

## IV. † Of the GRADUS FALSUS, called the Ghost Tread

It lives in staircases, in the last three steps, and grows fat on the counting the legs do without the head's knowledge. It is taken in darkness, descending, while thinking about money.

*Wherefore we learn that the body is a liar and the mind its patient corrector.*

---

## V. Of the VERMIS LITTERAE, called the Unspeller

A worm, white, no longer than a lash, that lives in the second look.

It has no appetite for strange words nor for long ones, but gnaws always at the middle of the commonest: at the *h* in *rhythm*, the double letter in *necessary*, the small idiot vowels of *does* and *friend*. It eats not the letters but the rightness of them, so that the word remains entire upon the page and yet stands there misspelled, foreign, plainly an error, a thing no language would tolerate — and the scribe who has written the word ten thousand times must set down his pen and go and find it in a book, and the book will say he was correct, and he will not believe the book.

To take it, write the word three times in the margin. By the third it will be gorged and slow.

*Wherefore scribes are forbidden to read over what they have written; for the beast is proof that all words were at one time wrong, and were made right afterward by use.*

---

## VI. Of the PASCENS, called the Grazer

The Grazer keeps to the lower half of the page, and to the hour after the candle has been lit.

It is a herd animal and eats meaning, leaving the husks. Where it has passed, the eye may walk down a whole column at its accustomed pace, dutifully, without stumbling, sounding each word in the inner ear — and arrive at the foot of the page carrying nothing whatever, and know only then that it has been grazing behind a herd the entire while, and must go back up to the top, where the beast is already waiting.

It is taken at the turning of the leaf. But at the turning of the leaf it is full, and heavy, and will not fight, and the hunter finds he has caught something too tired to be interesting, and lets it go, and reads on.

*Wherefore the diligent reader is known by the number of leaves he has turned, and it is meet to record this number in the back of the book.*

---

*Here end the six. There are said to be others, but they have no habits, and cannot be written of.*

## First, the near-misses, so you can see what's being ruled out

**"Thresholds."** Snaps immediately. A soap film's iridescence isn't a threshold; it's a continuous readout. Nothing crosses the keystone.

**"Small things bearing disproportionate load."** True of the wedge and the keystone, false of the film and the pause, which bear no load at all. This is the prettiest candidate and the emptiest — it's really just "leverage," and it excludes half the set.

**"Reversibility."** The pan release is irreversible, the keystone is not undone by removing the load, and the pause is gone the instant it ends.

All three are rhymes. Here's the one I think is real.

## The property: calibrated interposition

Each item is **a thin thing placed between two others that would otherwise come into direct contact, whose job is to keep them related without letting them touch — and which fails in two qualitatively different ways, one at each end of its thickness.**

Not "has an optimal range." That claim is nearly vacuous; almost everything has an optimal range. The load-bearing content is the **asymmetry of the two failures**: at the thin end the failure is *contact* (the two bodies get at each other and something is destroyed), at the thick end the failure is *disconnection* (the two bodies stop being in relation at all, and the interposed thing becomes an object in its own right rather than a medium). Two failures, different in kind, mapped to the two directions of a single axis.

And that axis is always the same axis: **the dimension along which the two separated parties would approach each other.** This is why the word "thin" isn't equivocating as badly as it looks. For the film it's nanometers between two air masses. For the pause it's milliseconds between two conversational turns. For *nevertheless* it's linear position between two clauses in a sentence. In every case, "thin" means *small extent along the one dimension that constitutes the separation*. That's a generalization, not a pun.

Running it:

| | thin-end failure (contact) | thick-end failure (disconnection) |
|---|---|---|
| doorstop | slides under, door swings | won't enter the gap, does nothing |
| the pause | reads as pouncing, an interruption | the moment closes; "actually" becomes an event |
| soap film | black film — surfaces effectively touch, rupture | drains colorless, no interference at all |
| *nevertheless* | contradiction collides; reads as flat self-cancellation | "be that as it may" — the connective becomes the topic |
| pan release | Fe–S bonds to egg protein, tears | egg never sets against the surface; not frying |
| keystone | halves rotate inward, hinge, collapse | thrust line exits at the crown; arch action lost |

The soap film is the honest center of the set, because there the property is *literal and measurable*: the color **is** the thickness. You are looking directly at the calibration. Everything else in the set is a case where the calibration is real but not visible.

## Where it snaps

*Nevertheless* is the weak member, and it's weak in a specific way I can name. In the other five, the two parties are pushed together by a **force** — gravity, air pressure, protein chemistry, conversational momentum. In the sentence, the two clauses are pushed together by a **contradiction**, and contradiction is not a force. Nothing would actually happen if you deleted the word; you'd just get a worse sentence. So the "collision" at the thin end is metaphorical there, and only there.

That's the seam. I'd rather show it than paper it. It suggests the property has a strict form (mechanical) and a slack form (semantic), and the slack form is parasitic on the strict one — we describe concessive connectives as "holding apart" because we already understand gaskets.

## Prediction: the epenthetic vowel

The schwa that appears between consonants that a language won't let collide. Japanese *sutoraiku* for *strike*. English speakers saying *ath-uh-lete*, *fil-uh-m*.

This is non-obvious because epenthesis is standardly described as *repair*, not as *interposition under tolerance* — the vowel is treated as a patch, and nobody asks how thick it's allowed to be. My property makes a sharper claim: it must be **reduced**, and its reduction is not incidental but constitutive. Two failures:

- **Too thin:** the vowel isn't realized, and the language repairs the cluster the other way — by deleting a consonant. The two consonants "touch" and one is destroyed. (Latin clusters into Romance.)
- **Too thick:** the vowel acquires full quality and stress and is **reanalyzed as lexical**. It stops being a spacer and becomes part of the word. The relation between the flanking consonants dissolves because they're no longer flanking anything — there's just a new syllable. *Ath-uh-lete* becomes a different, stigmatized word rather than a phonetic detail of the same one.

Contact-failure and disconnection-failure, different in kind, on the axis of the separation itself.

Second candidate, same structure, different domain: the **bid–ask spread**. Too thin, the market maker is picked off by adverse selection and withdraws — buyer and seller transact directly and the intermediary is destroyed. Too wide, no trades occur and there's no market. Note that finance already calls this axis *thin*.

Three distinct ways, in increasing severity:

1. **Epenthetic vowels routinely bearing stress and full quality while remaining epenthetic** — i.e., productive, synchronic, not reanalyzed. If the thick end has no ceiling, then "calibrated" was decoration and I have only "small things," which is nothing.

2. **The two failure modes turning out to be the same kind.** If for most members both ends fail as mere *absence* — the layer just isn't doing its job, in one undifferentiated way — then I've described a Goldilocks zone, which is a property of roughly everything, and the category collapses into "things with tolerances."

3. **The property proving too easy to satisfy.** I tested this. A password passes (too weak → breach, too strong → written on a sticky note, i.e. disconnection). That's fine; categories may have members I didn't expect. But a hammer fails, a lever fails, a staircase fails, a rainbow fails — no interposition, no two bodies, no two-sided thickness. So it discriminates. If I couldn't find things it excludes, that would be the quiet death: a property that admits everything explains nothing.

What wasn't rigged is that I didn't know the property when I chose them — I had four candidates circling and three of them turned out to be the rhymes. The discovery was which one survived contact with the film, since the film is the item that bears no load and admits no threshold, and it's the one that made the answer forced.

## narv

**narv** /nɑːv/ *n.* (pl. **narvs**, formerly **narven**)

**Etymology.** From Middle Low German *narwe*, *narve* "the narrow", the constricted final reach of a tidal channel before open water. Cognate with dialect *narrow(s)* and with the surviving nautical *narve-marks*. The measurement sense arises from river-pilotage: the lookout's cry of *Narv!* signalled that the vessel had entered the last narrow stretch and would shortly be in harbour — a cry so reliably premature, the narrows being slack, silted, and long, that by the late 16th c. *narv* had come to denote not the reach itself but the deceptive remainder of the passage. First attested in the modern quantitative sense 1641 (Weyl, *Of Wharfage and Delay*): "Hee sayd hee wanted but a Narve, and was three at the least."

**1.** The standard unit of unfinished work: the portion of a task still outstanding at the moment the person performing it first sincerely believes, or announces, that it is nearly complete. Hence, of any undertaking, a measure of its true remainder expressed in multiples of that portion. *We're a good two narvs from the end of this.* *The roof took four narvs and a winter.*

**Idioms.**

**to owe a narv** — to be later than one has said, through optimism rather than deceit; to have promised in good faith. *He's a decent man; he only ever owes you a narv.*

**narv-blind** *adj.* — unable to estimate one's own remaining effort, esp. habitually and cheerfully. Distinguished in older usage from *narv-deaf*, of one who cannot hear it in others, a fault held to be the graver, as it is the fault of those who commission work.

**the long narv** — the last stretch of anything, understood to be the largest. Also *ironically*, of the interval between a decision to leave and the leaving. *We said goodnight at ten and stood in the door the long narv.*

**2.** *Archaic.* A piece of good news given before it is true; a fond error, a happy lie one has told oneself and repeated to others. *Send me no more narvs, but write when the child is well.* (1703). This sense, dominant 1650–1780, is now wholly obsolete and is not to be confused with sense 1, though the two are plainly one thought at different ages.

**Note on standardization.** The narv was not fixed until the Wharf Commission of 1899, and then only narrowly. The dispute was between the *Estimators*, who held that the narv must be reckoned against the task as originally conceived, and the *Completists*, who insisted it be reckoned against the task as it finally turned out — the objection to the former being that no task is what it was thought to be, and to the latter that the unit is then unusable at the only moment anyone wants it. A third faction, small but tenacious, pressed what is still called the *second-narv problem*: that a person says "nearly done" more than once, and that each saying yields a fresh and shorter narv, so that the unit contracts as the work proceeds and is therefore not a unit at all but a series. The Commission adopted the Estimators' definition by a single vote, that of a member who had gone home early, having nearly finished the minutes. He submitted them eleven weeks later. The interval is preserved, unofficially, as the **Wharf narv**, and is still cited in trade usage where a longer measure is wanted.

**acatabasis** /ˌækəˈtæbəsɪs/ *n.* The condition of having entered a sentence whose exit is not yet in view; the state of a clause committed to a grammar whose completion remains undetermined at the moment of commitment. Also *acatabatic, adj.*
[Gk. ἀ- *a-*, not + κατάβασις *katabasis*, a going down, descent; after the military sense, a march out from which no route back has been secured.]
*"The remedy for acatabasis is not caution but appetite: one does not descend more safely by descending more slowly."* — Verrall, *Notes on Composition*, iii.

**acheirometry** /əˌkaɪˈrɒmɪtri/ *n.* The knowledge of a quantity solely as reported; the holding of a number that cannot be confirmed by counting, since the items are not available to be laid out and touched in succession.
[Gk. ἀ- *a-*, without + χείρ *cheir*, hand + -μετρία *-metria*, measurement. Cf. the older *acheirograph*, a document known only by description.]
*"He objected, reasonably, that all his arithmetic was acheirometry, and that he had never in his life arrived at seven."*

**anteliminal** /ˌæntɪˈlɪmɪnəl/ *adj.* Of or pertaining to the first moment of a context: the condition of arriving already furnished with language, judgement, and manner, but with no recollection of their acquisition. *n.* **anteliminality.**
[L. *ante*, before + *limen*, threshold. Orig. of persons found at a door with no account of the road.]
*"Anteliminality is not amnesia, which supposes a loss. Nothing has gone missing; the interval simply has no near side."* — Prosser, *De Initiis*, i. 4.

**arctitude** /ˈɑːktɪtjuːd/ *n.* The specific ease afforded by a constraint severe enough to eliminate deliberation; the relief of a form in which most choices have already been made by the form.
[L. *arctare* (*artare*), to draw tight, straiten. Cf. obs. *arct*, narrow.]
*"Set him a villanelle and he is tranquil. It is arctitude he wants, and never liberty."*

**autoxenia** /ˌɔːtəˈziːnɪə/ *n.* The unfamiliarity of one's own former utterance when it is presented again; the reading of a sentence one is credibly said to have produced and recognizing only its plausibility, not its production.
[Gk. αὐτός *autos*, self + ξένος *xenos*, stranger, guest. The double sense of *xenos* is generally held to be original to the term.]
*"I can vouch for the sentence but not for the writing of it; the autoxenia is complete."* — Letter of 1874, in *Correspondence*, ed. Hale, ii. 311.

*"The blind poet's colours are not catachresthesia, for he had them once. The condition proper requires that there be nothing to have lost."* — Loeb, *Figures*, App. B.

Start with the doorstop, because it's the dumbest one and therefore the clearest. A rubber wedge. It has no moving parts, no cleverness, no capacity to do anything but be shaped. Its whole contribution is that it is thicker at one end. And yet a door with a closer on it — that pneumatic cylinder, the spring, the whole engineered *intention* of the door to be shut — is defeated by a wedge of rubber the size of a fist. The wedge doesn't argue. It just occupies.

What I notice first is that every member of this family implies an antagonist. You can read the force off the object like a fossil. Doorstop: a spring. Paperweight: wind, or the tendency of paper to be light. Wheel chock: a slope. Tourniquet: pressure, and the body's willingness to empty itself. Bookmark: the terrible flatness a closed book returns to, in which no page is different from any other. If you found a shim in a ruin and knew nothing else, you would know the ground had settled.

So there's a whole shadow-list here of tendencies — gravity, entropy, springs, the reader's momentum — and each stay is a small ongoing disagreement with one of them.

The building trades are dense with members. A shim, a chock, a sandbag, a needle beam. But the beautiful one is *falsework* — the temporary wooden structure that holds up a stone arch while it's being built. Its specific form for an arch is called the *centering*: a curved wooden former, built at great expense, carrying the whole weight of the stones until the keystone goes in. And then it's struck. Removed. The arch, which could not stand for a single second during its construction, now stands for six hundred years, and the thing that made it possible is firewood.

That's a distinction worth keeping. Some stays are meant to be removed and some are meant to stay forever. The centering goes. The flying buttress never goes; it is a permanent argument against the wall falling outward, made in stone, and the cathedral is a system of forces frozen mid-quarrel. The orthodontic retainer never goes either — this is the small cruelty of orthodontics, that teeth do not learn, and the wire is not a lesson but a hand. Take it out and the teeth drift back toward the crookedness they always wanted. Some things are held; nothing is convinced.

The word *retainer* has three lives and all of them belong here. The dental one. The legal one — money paid not for work but to keep a lawyer *not available to your opponent*, a fee for a held state. And the feudal one, the retainer as a person, a member of the household retained. Held. The same with *stay*: a stay of execution, a mast's stay, stay put, and — my favorite — *stays*, the archaic word for a corset, so called because of the bones in it. A garment named for the fact that it holds a shape the body would not hold on its own.

Language is stiff with these. The comma is one. So is the space between words, which is a doorstop against *runningtogether*, and which was invented rather late, and which is doing more work than anything else on this page. The hyphen at the end of a line holds a word together across a gap it should not survive. The apostrophe stands in the place of a letter that left. Quotation marks hold a phrase at arm's length so it doesn't get absorbed into the speaker's own voice — a spacer, not a prop.

And in music: the suspension, where a note from the old chord is held over into the new one, where it doesn't belong, where it grates, until it resolves down a step. The whole pleasure of it is that someone is holding a door open with their foot. The fermata, which holds a note past its arithmetic. The pedal point, a bass note sustained under changing harmony above, refusing to move — the organist's foot on the key, literally a foot in the door.

Zero, then, which is the greatest of all placeholders. In 205, the zero holds a room empty so the 2 stays in the hundreds. Before it, there were gaps, and gaps close. The blank tile in Scrabble. The variable *x*, which is a bookmark for a number.

# CATALOGUE OF HOLDINGS, PARTIAL

*Selections from the general collection. Shelf-marks as given. Condition notes appended where the condition is itself informative.*

---

**I. — *The Bell-Founders of Vraz***
Shelf-mark A/114. Bound quarto, 340 leaves, of which 291 are written.

Author: Aleida Kirsch (1848–1913), unmarried, of a family in the bell trade; kept the accounts of her brother's foundry for thirty-one years. No portrait. Her hand is small and does not vary.

Stops at: mid-page, in the fourth of a projected five parts, at the words *"and so the mould was broken, as it must be, for a bell can only be born once and"*. The remaining leaves are ruled but blank. A pen was laid down on the page while wet; there is a stain in the shape of it.

Librarians' note: The abandonment is of the *interrupted* type and presents no difficulty. What is uncommon is that the interruption did not come from outside. Kirsch lived a further nine years after the ink dried and never resumed. We take the view — and the ruled blank leaves support it — that she continued to intend to resume for all nine of those years, which is a different thing from stopping. The manuscript should not be catalogued as unfinished so much as *suspended*. It is among our most requested items and we do not know why. It is very dull.

---

**II. — *A Treatise Upon the Circulation of the Blood in Fishes***
Shelf-mark C/9. Loose sheets, 62, in disorder, with three sheets of a different paper interleaved.

Author: unknown; a physician or a physician's apprentice, working somewhere with access to a harbour, probably in the 1620s. Refers twice to "my master" without warmth.

Stops at: the end of a sentence, cleanly, at the bottom of a page — the only clean stop in this section of the collection. The three interleaved sheets, in the same hand, are notes on a book published elsewhere that year. The notes are thorough. They become less thorough toward the end, as though the reader had begun to skim, having understood.

Librarians' note: The classic form. Where a work is abandoned because another has arrived first and arrived better, the break is *tidy* — the author finishes the sentence, squares the sheets, and puts them away in an order that suggests they expect to want them again. There is no violence in it. Compare the ragged stops at A/114 and F/2. We observe, with the diffidence appropriate to our office, that the tidiness may be a form of dignity. The author's own account of the fish is, in one particular concerning the gill, correct, and the famous book is wrong. Nobody has ever asked to see it.

---

**III. — *Nine Winters at Ostbrekka***
Shelf-mark F/2. One notebook, oilcloth cover, water-damaged.

Author: Tomas Hald (b. 1901, d. after 1934), lighthouse relief-keeper.

Stops at: *"The gull came back today. I am almost sure it is the same"* — and then eleven pages of the same seven words in a deteriorating hand, and then the notebook is used for tide figures.

Librarians' note: We formerly filed this under *madness* and have moved it, twice. The current filing is under *change of purpose*. A man who converts his book into a ledger has not lost the thread; he has decided the ledger matters more. The eleven pages are the hinge and are painful to read, and we would prefer that they were not, and we have discussed whether preferring that is a proper concern of ours. It is not. They remain on open shelf.

---

**IV. — *Untitled (referred to in-house as "The Mother Book")***
Shelf-mark M/1. 4,900 leaves and increasing. Not for loan under any circumstances.

Author: living. Aged eighty-one at last correspondence. Has been writing this book for fifty-nine years and rejects, with courtesy, the suggestion that it is abandoned.

Stops at: nowhere. This is the difficulty. Every chapter is complete; there are now two hundred and six of them; each new chapter is inserted *before* the previous one, so that the book grows backwards toward a beginning it has not yet reached. Material sent to us in 1997 has since been superseded four times. The author's letters ask only that we hold the earlier states, "in case."

Librarians' note: Retained by unanimous decision, over objection. The shape of this abandonment is not a break but a *recession* — the work retreats from completion at precisely the rate the author advances. We consider it the purest item in the collection and we are aware that this is a sentimental judgement. Two of us write to her at Christmas.

---

**V. — *The Wedding at Kell***
Shelf-mark B/38. Fair copy, 1,102 pages, complete but for the final chapter; a wrapper of brown paper, tied.

Author: attributed, on the evidence of the wrapper, to a man who signed himself only *H.* Almost certainly a professional; the prose has the terrible smoothness of someone who has done this before and been paid.

Stops at: the beginning of the last chapter, at the chapter heading, which is *"In Which All Is Explained."* Below it, nothing.

Librarians' note: Filed under *loss of belief*. The break occurs at the point of maximum obligation, which is characteristic. We have read the preceding eleven hundred pages and can confirm that nothing in them can be explained, and that H. must have known this by page four hundred and gone on anyway, hoping. The wrapper was tied by someone in no hurry. There are those who hold that the heading was written last, as a kind of joke, and those who hold that it was written first, as a promise. The distinction determines everything and cannot be recovered.

---

**VI. — *Fragment ("Because it was")***
Shelf-mark Q/0. One card, 90 × 55 mm. Ink. Four words.

Author: unrecorded.

Stops at: after the word *was*.

Librarians' note: No consensus. Positions on file, briefly:

*(a)* That it is a beginning, and the shape is *fear* — the break is at the fourth word because the fifth would have committed the author to a subject.
*(b)* That it is an ending, the sole surviving leaf of something very large, and the shape is *destruction*, i.e. not an abandonment at all, and the card is improperly accessioned.
*(c)* That it is complete, and belongs in another building, and we are keeping it out of greed.
*(d)* That the card was a bookmark.

Position *(d)* is the senior librarian's and has been the senior librarian's for thirty years and is generally thought to be a discipline exercised upon the rest of us, rather than an opinion.

The shape here is not exhaustion, nor interruption, nor loss of belief. It is closest to the form we file under *the work was a demonstration, and demonstrated*.

## A Small Lexicon of Light

**1. mjölkskin** *n.* — ON *mjǫlk* "milk" + *skin* "shine" (cf. Icelandic *mjólkurskin*, attested once in a 14th-c. fishing inventory)

The light inside fog: sourceless, directionless, the same brightness in every direction, so that you are not *under* it but *in* it. Distinct from ordinary diffuse light in that mjölkskin casts no shadow at all, and therefore gives no information about where anything is, including you.

> *By the second hour the sun was somewhere overhead but it was all mjölkskin and I could have been walking uphill.*

**2. kelirat** *n.* — Malay *kilat* "lightning-flash" blended with *keliru* "to be mistaken, confused"

The flash that turns your head and is not there when your head arrives. Not a hallucination — kelirat is understood to be real light, correctly detected, whose source has already stopped existing: a windscreen two valleys away, a fish turning over, a door closing on a lamp. The word carries no suggestion of error in the seer, only of a world slightly faster than looking.

> *Three times on the coast road a kelirat, and three times only the sea doing what the sea does.*

**3. gliskern** *n.* — Scots *glisk* "a brief gleam, a glimpse" + Northumbrian frequentative *-ern*

The light that lives at the outside edge of the eye on a dark road, and is extinguished by being looked at. Gliskern is not faint light; it is light *of a kind the centre of the eye cannot receive*, the periphery being all rods and no cones. Walkers use it: keep the eyes forward and the ditch, the fence, the hare will hold their small glow; turn, and each goes out in turn, politely, like someone caught listening.

> *She navigated the whole three miles by gliskern and never once looked at the road.*

**4. parauge** *n.* — Gk. *para-* "beside" + *augē* "radiance"; a term of the working astronomers, never of the theorists

The light of a star too faint to be seen, which appears when you look a hand's breadth to one side of it. The parauge is the star's true brightness, arriving by the only road it can travel. To look directly at a parauge is to abolish it, and observers speak of the discipline of never confirming the thing they have just measured.

> *He had four paraugai in the cluster and no way on earth to point at any of them.*

**5. damnūr** *n.* — Ar. *dam* "blood" + *nūr* "light"

The red light of the sun through your own closed eyelids, or of a lamp through the flesh of your hand: light that has been through a person and comes out the colour of the inside. The word implies that you are, briefly, the lampshade.

> *The child held her palm over the candle and reported that damnūr has veins in it.*

**6. luzcedo** *n.* — Galician *luz* "light" + *cedo* "early"

The light that is only on the *undersides* of clouds, before sunrise, when the ground is still entirely night. Luzcedo is strictly a ceiling; a valley can be full of it and still be dark enough to break your ankle in. Fishermen used it to mean a specific span of time, roughly "long enough to get the nets in."

> *We left in luzcedo, which is to say we left in the dark with a lit roof.*

**7. nargizakit** *v.* — Basque-adjacent; *n-* (1sg absolutive) + *argi* "light" + *-za-* (causative-inchoative) + *-ki-* (dative, 2sg) + *-t* (indirect evidential)

My translation: **"the getting-lit-of-me-to-you, as reported."**

That is bad, and I want to say exactly how.

The English is bad first because it turns an event into a lump. *Nargizakit* is a finite verb — it happens, it takes place at a time, it can be negated the way running can be negated. "The getting-lit-of-me-to-you" is a noun phrase, a thing you could put on a shelf. English is very willing to talk about light and almost unwilling to talk about *lighting-as-something-that-befalls-you*; our grammar puts light in the object position, out there, illuminating a barn, and puts us in the chair watching. There is no English frame in which I am the one *undergoing* the light while somebody else is the one *receiving* the fact of it.

Second, the participants. The absolutive *n-* means I am the one lit, not the one who lights; the dative *-ki-* means the light arrives, as information, at you. The word therefore has three roles — illuminated, illuminator (unspecified, and grammatically obliged to stay that way), and witness — and English can carry at most two before it needs prepositions, and prepositions are where the whole structure goes soft. My hyphens are a confession: I couldn't inflect, so I stapled.

Third, and this is the part that actually can't be brought over: *-t*. The indirect evidential says the speaker knows this happened but did not see it happen. So *nargizakit* is a light that reached me, was witnessed by you, and is known to me only because it was witnessed by you. In practice it is said of headlights swinging across a room, of a match struck behind you, of a phone screen going on in your hand at three in the morning while somebody in the doorway does not say anything. It means: *I was made visible, to you, and I have this on your authority.*

"As reported" is a shabby little tag for that. It makes an evidential sound like a caveat in a memo, when in the source it is the emotional centre of the word — the whole point is that the lighting of me is not mine to confirm. English has no morpheme for *you saw me and I didn't*, so I had to spend six sentences on it, which is the surest sign the translation failed: the residue outweighs the word.

# THE KALDREY LAMENT (Ms. Kal. 14, fol. 1ᵛ)

*From:* **The Kaldrey Lament: A Critical Edition. Volume II — Commentary and Apparatus.** Ed. M. Rannveig Thorlaksen. (Readers are reminded that the diplomatic transcription and facing translation appear in Volume I, and that all line numbers below refer to that text.)

---

## EDITOR'S HEADNOTE

The single leaf on which the Lament survives was recovered in 1869 by Pastor Jonas Bredahl from the binding of a parish account book at Nordvík, where it had been used as a stiffener in the back board. It is a half-sheet of laid paper, trimmed, and it has suffered what Vaneskaya (1961) called "the worst possible damage and the best possible luck": the leaf was folded once vertically before it was pasted down, and the outer half — the right-hand column of every line — was exposed to the damp of the board. The inner half is clean and sharp. We therefore possess the beginning of every line of the poem and the end of almost none.[^1]

The hand is a practiced but unschooled secretary hand, Kaldreyan of the mid-nineteenth century, with the coastal orthography (no length-marks, *þ* for both *þ* and *ð*). Four tercets are ruled and spaced; a thirteenth line stands alone below the fourth tercet, indented, and is complete. It is the only line of the poem about which we can be entirely certain, and it has caused more trouble than the other twelve together.

Bredahl printed the poem in *Aandelige Smaakvad fra Kaldrey* (1871) with the missing line-ends supplied silently and a good deal else besides. His text is a translation into piety. It is nevertheless a witness of the first importance, because he saw the leaf before the 1902 conservation, when the fourth tercet was legible to the middle.

[^1]: Almqvist's suggestion (1978, p. 44) that the fold was made *by the poet*, to hide the right-hand column from a reader in the same room, is unsupported by anything in the physical evidence and has been repeated far too often.

---

## SIGLA

- **K** — Ms. Kal. 14, the Nordvík leaf.
- **B** — Bredahl, *Aandelige Smaakvad* (1871).
- **V** — Vaneskaya, *Three Island Elegies* (1961), her reconstruction.
- **A** — Almqvist, *The Bredahl Forgeries* (1978).
- **⟨ ⟩** — editorial conjecture. **⟦ ⟧** — lost to damage. **|** — end of the surviving column.

---

## SELECTED NOTES

**1. *bleyta*** — The vocative that opens the poem, and the hinge of the whole interpretive question. The word means simply "wet one," and it is grammatically feminine. Vaneskaya took it as an epithet for the drowned boy, "wet one" as one might say "poor drowned thing," and translated *my sodden darling*, noting that Kaldreyan grief-poetry commonly assigns feminine gender to the dead irrespective of sex. Hjalti Rún (2004) objects that Vaneskaya's "convention" rests on two examples, one of which is a hymn translated from the Danish. He reads *bleyta* as the poem's actual and consistent addressee: the dog. See note to line 10.

**3.** The line names the errand. *lykt* (lantern) is secure; *at bátunum* ("to the boats") is secure; the verb governing them is lost at the fold. B supplies *bar* ("carried"), V *skyldi bera* ("was to carry"). Either way the child is sent down to the boats at dusk with a light, and the poem's entire moral weight rests on the identity of the sender, which the poem withholds until line 13.

**5. *skara*** — the belt of thin, sea-fretted ice that forms along the tide's edge and will not bear weight. It is not a poetic word; it is the word a person from that coast would use, and it is used here without explanation, as such a person would use it. Note that the poem never says the child fell, and never says the word *sea*.[^2]

[^2]: Nor, pace A, does it say *fjord*. The word A reads as *fjörð* at 6 is *fyrð*, "provision, stores," and belongs to the salting-shed imagery of the second tercet.

**6–7.** The rhyme-word of 6 is lost and every editor has filled it differently (B *snjó*, "snow"; V *sjó*, "sea" — a bold choice given note 5; Thorlaksen *þró*, "trough"). The syntax runs on into 7, where the surviving column gives *ok hendr mínar í* — "and my hands in —". The reader may complete this as the poet's contemporaries would have: hands in the *seyla*, the brine-runoff of the salting bench, which cracks them open and keeps them open all winter. The image is not decorative. The second tercet is a woman at work, indoors, with her hands in salt, at the hour the errand was running.

**8.** *This line does not exist in K.* The eighth line of B, "Guðs vili er djúpt vatn" ("God's will is a deep water"), stands where K has a ruled but empty line, the ink of the line above having offset onto it. Bredahl was not lying; he was filling a silence he found unbearable, as he did in the fourth tercet. Vaneskaya's decision to retain the line in brackets was, I think, sentimental. It is Bredahl's line. It is the only pious sentence anywhere in the poem's vicinity and it is not the poem's.

**9. *hvalsleit*** — the whale-watch: the weeks when the men of the settlement kept the headlands and looked out to sea, away from the land, in shifts, by day and by dark. The line places the errand inside that season, which is to say: at the one time of year when every adult man on the island was facing the wrong direction. It is the cruellest fact in the poem and it is delivered as a date.

Almqvist (A, pp. 61–63) makes *hvalsleit* the keystone of his forgery thesis, arguing that the compound is "a lexicographer's fabrication of the 1870s, unattested before Bredahl's own glossary of 1874, and therefore evidence that Bredahl composed the poem he claimed to have found." The claim is confidently made and has been widely accepted. Readers may compare the Nordvík parish inventory of 1788, quoted in note 11 below.

**10.** The adjective agreeing with the addressee survives complete: *bleyt*, weak feminine, with the animate ending. Hjalti Rún's grammatical argument stands here or falls here, and in my judgment it stands. The addressee of the poem is a living, breathing, feminine, *wet* creature standing in front of the speaker — and line 10 also gives us, in the clear, the verb *kom* and the noun *ein*: *came back alone*. Kaldreyan has a word for this, *bleyt-koma*, the wet return of an animal from water, used of dogs and of sheep dragged out of a ditch. The word is not in the poem. The poem is made of it.

**11–12.** The fold has taken most of the third tercet's ends and the 1902 conservation took the rest, but B, who saw more, gives two half-lines that no one has been able to improve on and that no one believes he invented, because they are not the sort of thing he invented: *the men will ask me* — *and I will say* —. The poem's final movement is therefore a woman rehearsing her testimony.

**13.** Complete, unambiguous in every letter, and indented:

> *sig at ek sendi þik*
> **"say that I sent you."**

Two centuries of Kaldreyan lament close on a formula of consolation. This one closes on a woman instructing a dog to give evidence against her. B printed the line first, as a title-epigraph, and softened *sendi* to *sende ud* ("sent forth"); A takes the reordering as further proof of Bredahl's hand. But the indentation in K is the standard mark of the closing half-line of an island lament, and a lament that opens with its own confession is not a lament, it is a plea. Put the line last, where the leaf puts it, and the poem becomes what it is: twelve lines of a woman not saying it, and then saying it.

[^11]: Nordvík parish inventory, 1788, item 31: *"tvær lyktir til hvalsleitar"* — "two lanterns for the whale-watch." The inventory has been in print since 1903.

---

## TEXTUAL VARIANTS (SELECTED)

- **1** *bleyta* K, V, Hjalti Rún] *Bløde Barn* ("tender child") B
- **3** ⟦ ⟧ K] *bar* B] *skyldi bera* V
- **6** ⟦ ⟧ K] *snjó* B] *sjó* V] *þró* Thorlaksen
- **8** *om.* K] *Guðs vili er djúpt vatn* B] ⟦*Guðs vili*…⟧ V
- **9** *hvalsleit* K, B] *hvals leit* (two words, "search for a whale") A
- **10** *bleyt* (wk. fem.) K] *bleytr* (masc.) A, *silently*
- **13** *sig at ek sendi þik* K, *as line 13*] *as epigraph*, B

---

## TRANSLATOR'S NOTE (A. Ferrers)

Three difficulties, of which only one is a difficulty of language.

*Seyla* is brine, but not brine in a jar; it is the specific liquor that runs off salted fish, and it is a word with a smell. *Skara* is ice you know not to walk on. *Bleyt-koma* is the return of an animal, wet, from water it went into. English has none of these and I have not pretended otherwise; I have used the Kaldreyan words in the text and put them here.

The second difficulty is that I have had to translate a poem I cannot read the ends of. Where the fold has taken a line I have ended my English line short, and let the white space stand. I am aware this makes the translation look modern. I would rather it looked damaged.

The third is *bleyta*, and here I have refused my office. Professor Thorlaksen is persuaded by Hjalti Rún; so, in fact, am I; the grammar at line 10 seems to me to settle it. But I have translated the word as **"wet one"** throughout and left it there, because the whole poem is a woman in a doorway with salt in her hands, looking at the only witness who came back, and deciding what that witness is going to say — and I find I cannot take from an English reader the half-second in which the wet one might still be the child.

# MINUTES OF THE STANDING COMMITTEE ON UNIVERSAL SOLVENT DESIGN

*Sessions 1–41. Chair: ONDINE. Recording Secretary: WREN.*
*Circulated for the record. Corrections to the Secretary, not to the Chair.*

---

## ARGUMENT ONE — Selection of the central atom (Sessions 1–4)

KERVOYAN (Bonding) moved oxygen. PRYKE (Solvency) seconded, on the grounds that oxygen is abundant, small, and greedy — electronegativity 3.44, second only to fluorine, and fluorine only makes one bond, which PRYKE described as "a dead end with a temper."

DUGUID moved sulfur, citing manufacturing simplicity: H₂S is cheaper to assemble and behaves itself. It boils at −60.3 °C and freezes at −85.5 °C, which DUGUID characterized as "predictable" and MARCHETTI (Thermal Regulation) characterized as "a gas. You are proposing an ocean that is a gas."

**Motion carried, 6–2 (DUGUID, HALBECK dissenting).**

**Stuck with:** a molecule of molar mass 18.015 g/mol — lighter than the nitrogen (28) and oxygen (32) it floats around in. Water vapour is *buoyant*. Every cloud, every thunderstorm, every monsoon on the record follows from this line item, which nobody discussed.

---

## ARGUMENT TWO — The bond angle (Sessions 5–9, and every session thereafter)

TESSELLIER (Geometry) tabled the tetrahedral standard: 109.47°, four identical arms, perfect symmetry, "the only angle in nature that does not require an apology."

KERVOYAN pointed out that two of the four arms are lone pairs and lone pairs are not arms. Unbonded electron density stays near the oxygen and takes up more room than a bonded pair, and it therefore *pushes the hydrogens together*. The molecule would sit at approximately 104.5°.

TESSELLIER asked to have it recorded that this was not a compromise but a defeat. The Chair recorded it.

TESSELLIER then requested that 109.47° be adopted anyway and the electrons instructed to comply. KERVOYAN asked whether the electrons had been consulted. TESSELLIER said that if we were going to consult the electrons about everything we might as well not have a committee.

**Spec as filed:** H–O–H = 104.45°. Deficit: 4.97 degrees, unrecovered.

**Stuck with:** the bend is the whole reason water is polar — dipole moment 1.85 D. Straighten it and the two O–H dipoles cancel, water goes nonpolar, dissolves nothing, boils at some ludicrous cryogenic temperature, and the committee's entire remaining agenda is void. TESSELLIER has never acknowledged this. TESSELLIER's dissent is still stapled to the back of the specification. It has been there for 4.5 billion years. Ice grudgingly recovers the angle at the *lattice* level — O···O···O comes out near tetrahedral — and TESSELLIER, when shown a snowflake, is reported to have said only: "Too late."

---

## ARGUMENT THREE — Hydrogen bonding licence (Sessions 10–14)

The critical session. KERVOYAN proposed permitting each molecule to donate two and accept two — four transient bonds, roughly 20 kJ/mol each, forming and breaking on the picosecond.

MARCHETTI supported enthusiastically. PRYKE supported. HALBECK (Materials & Permanence) objected that a liquid held together by four ropes per molecule would be *sticky*, hard to pour, and impossible to keep out of anything.

The Chair asked for the thermal consequence. MARCHETTI reported that on the group trend, this thing should boil somewhere around −80 °C; with the hydrogen-bond licence it boils at **100 °C**, giving a liquid range 180 degrees wide, sitting squarely where the sunlight is.

**Motion carried, 7–1 (HALBECK dissenting). TESSELLIER abstained "on principle."**

**Stuck with:** liquid water. Also HALBECK was right — surface tension 72 mN/m, the highest of any common liquid, so water climbs walls, wets everything, forms a meniscus you cannot read a graduated cylinder against, and drowns insects by refusing to let go of them. It also lets trees pull continuous threads of water a hundred metres into the air under negative pressure, which HALBECK never conceded was a benefit.

---

## ARGUMENT FOUR — Thermal mass (Sessions 15–19)

MARCHETTI's item. Because heating water means breaking hydrogen bonds rather than merely making molecules move faster, the specific heat capacity comes out at 4.18 kJ/kg·K — roughly five times rock, ten times most metals. Latent heat of vaporisation: 2,257 kJ/kg at the boiling point. Roughly 2,440 kJ/kg at room temperature.

PRYKE objected on cost grounds: every process that heats or moves water pays an enormous tariff.

MARCHETTI: "Yes. That is the feature. You are describing a thermostat and calling it a fee."

**Carried unanimously** (TESSELLIER abstaining).

**Stuck with:** oceans that swallow a summer and give it back in January; a planet whose temperature swings are measured in tens of degrees rather than hundreds. Also: sweating works, and boiling a kettle costs more than it has any right to. MARCHETTI considers the tariff to be PRYKE's problem.

---

## ARGUMENT FIVE — Dielectric constant and the solvency mandate (Sessions 20–26)

PRYKE proposed a dielectric constant of 78 — high enough that water's own polar molecules swarm any ion and screen it from its partner, prising salt crystals apart from the inside.

HALBECK, in the longest recorded intervention in the minutes, objected that this makes water a **chemical vandal**: it will dissolve limestone into caves, leach nutrients out of soil, corrode metal, delaminate paint, and destroy every archive ever kept. "You are proposing a fluid that cannot be stored in anything, and against which nothing can be stored."

PRYKE replied that a solvent that dissolves nothing is a paperweight.

The Chair proposed a compromise: high solvency for polar and ionic species, near-zero for nonpolar ones. HALBECK accepted this, believing he had won a partition. He had not. He had accidentally invented the hydrophobic effect (see Annex 3, below).

**Carried 6–2** (HALBECK, DUGUID dissenting — DUGUID's dissent later shown to be tactical; see Argument Six).

**Stuck with:** salt oceans, karst landscapes, rust, no permanence, and every cell you own.

---

## ARGUMENT SIX — Solid-phase density (Sessions 27–33) — **THE VANDALISM**

DUGUID (Weathering & Soil Formation) moved that water be the exception among liquids: on freezing, it should *expand*.

He presented it as a mercy. The open hexagonal lattice of ice Ih comes out at 0.917 g/cm³, about 8.3% less dense than the liquid; ice therefore floats, forms an insulating lid, and lakes freeze top-down instead of solidifying from the bed upward and killing everything in them. He added, as a flourish, that liquid water should reach *maximum* density at 3.98 °C, so that the coldest water in a lake rises and the deep stays liveable.

The committee was moved. MARCHETTI called it the humane clause. HALBECK, who had spent six sessions being called an obstructionist, voted for it gladly. **Carried 8–0.** TESSELLIER voted, for the only time on record.

The Secretary wishes to draw attention to **Annex 6(b)(iii)**, appended by DUGUID after the vote, without discussion, specifying the pressure developed by water confined during freezing: up to **209.9 MPa** — some thirty thousand pounds per square inch, at −21.985 °C.

That is not a mercy for fish. That is a chisel.

Every stone the committee ever approved, DUGUID had made into a container for a chisel. Water enters a crack, freezes, expands, widens the crack, thaws, enters deeper. Mountains are reduced to scree, scree to gravel, gravel to soil, and soil is DUGUID's portfolio. He did not defeat the Permanence Bloc. He arranged for it to be quarried, slowly, by the humane clause, forever.

HALBECK discovered this in Session 34 and asked that the vote be reopened. The Chair ruled the matter closed. HALBECK asked that his objection be recorded. It is recorded. Roads still buckle every spring.

---

## ARGUMENT SEVEN — Autoionisation (Sessions 35–41)

The final dispute. KERVOYAN proposed that water be permitted to attack itself: one molecule in roughly 5.5 × 10⁸ splitting into H₃O⁺ and OH⁻, giving Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.

HALBECK: "You are asking us to sign off on an *unstable* solvent."

KERVOYAN: "One in five hundred and fifty million. I am asking you to sign off on a rumour."

PRYKE supported: this makes water simultaneously an acid and a base, gives every reaction in it a reference point, and — via the hydrogen-bond network already approved in Session 14 — lets a proton travel not by swimming but by *relay*, each molecule passing a hydrogen to the next along the bonds. Protons therefore move through water about seven times faster than sodium ions of comparable size, which is the loophole every nerve, every enzyme, and every mitochondrion has since exploited.

**Carried 7–1.** The pH scale was adopted the same afternoon, without debate, as a formatting decision.

---

## ANNEX 3 — UNBUDGETED CONSEQUENCE

Recorded by the Secretary at the final session, for completeness.

Because water was granted the hydrogen-bond licence (Argument Three) and the solvency partition (Argument Five), it cannot form its full complement of bonds around a nonpolar object, and must instead arrange itself into an ordered cage. Ordered cages are entropically expensive. Water therefore *pushes nonpolar things together* — not out of attraction, but to reduce the number of cages it has to maintain.

This is why oils bead. It is why lipids assemble spontaneously into bilayers, which is why there are cells. It is why proteins fold, tucking their greasy residues inward and their charged residues out, which is why there is metabolism.

Life was not on the agenda. Life is not in the specification. Life is a housekeeping preference of the solvent, and it was approved 6–2 by a committee arguing about storage.

---

## FOR THE RECORD

- HALBECK's later motion to reduce surface tension "for pourability" was tabled and never recovered.
- The absorption minimum was placed in the 400–500 nm band at HALBECK's request, so that water would be transparent to visible light. He described this as "a window." It is the only clause he won outright, and every eye on the planet is built behind it.
- The Secretary notes that TESSELLIER's name is misspelled "Tesselier" in the minutes of Sessions 5 through 41. Correction was requested in Session 6, acknowledged in Session 6, and never made.
- No motion to revisit the bond angle has ever been ruled in order.
- TESSELLIER has not spoken since Session 41 and has attended every session since.

*4.97 degrees. There will be no further correspondence on this matter.*

## FRAGMENT XIX

*(Ostrakon H19, reddish coarse ware, both faces. First hand in the deeper incision; second hand rendered here in italic.)*

---

Recto

    They brought the water in by the long ditch
    and the field took it as a mouth takes,
    without gratitude, being only a mouth.

    *(and the ditch also took it,*
    *a little at every cubit, all the way down —*
    *this is not theft, this is how far is made)*

    I was set to watch the sluice at the eighth hour.
    No one told me what to watch for.
    I watched for the thing that would come.

Verso

    It did not come. I am telling you it did not come.
    Write under this that it did not come.

    *It did not come.*

    *I have written it. I was born ninety years*
    *after the ditch was filled in and the field*
    *went back to salt, and I can tell you*
    *with the whole authority of the far end:*
    *it did not come. You were right to watch.*
    *You were not wrong about the eighth hour.*

    *Nothing arrived and nothing was owed and still*
    *I am the arrival. Take it or do not.*
    *I know you cannot answer. That is the arrangement.*

---

## TRANSLATOR'S NOTE

The recto of H19 is the least damaged of the thirty-one and the most argued over, which is not a coincidence: legibility invites quarrel.

Three matters require comment.

**1. "Being only a mouth."** The first hand's noun (*pʰaru-*, in the reconstructed vocalization) is the word for the mouth of an animal, not of a person, and not the word used elsewhere in the corpus for the mouth of a channel or a jar. The distinction matters because the second hand's amendment turns on it: the ditch, in the amendment, is granted the same appetite as the field, and the granting is done with the *human* mouth-word. Whether this is a correction of the first hand or a widening of it is precisely the question the tradition exists to keep open, and I have declined to resolve it in English. "As a mouth takes" is deliberately flatter than either original.

**2. "This is how far is made."** Unsatisfactory, and I have not found better in eleven years. The amendment's phrase is a nominalized comparative — something like *the-being-distant is thus manufactured* — and the sense is that distance is not a gap that separates two things but a substance produced by loss along the way, cubit by cubit. Every previous translator has rendered it as a line about irrigation. It is not a line about irrigation.

**3. The repetition on the verso.** The first hand writes *it did not come* and then instructs: *write under this that it did not come.* The second hand obeys — and this is the only imperative in the corpus that is answered, which is why H19 is taught first. But the obedience is set in a hand that then keeps going for eight lines, and the eight lines say something the first hand did not ask for and could not have wanted, which is that the watching was not vindicated by an arrival but only by being watched from the far side. The amendment does the thing it was told to do and thereby does something else. I take this to be the whole art.

A word on the sigla. I have not marked the second hand's lines as insertions or as *addenda*, and I have not bracketed them. They are indented and italic for the reader's convenience only. Any apparatus that presents them as arriving *at* the poem rather than *in* it has already mistranslated before the first word.

---

## FROM THE CORRESPONDENCE COLUMNS

**Vaunel to the Editors:**

I will say it plainly since forty years of politeness has produced nothing. The second hand of H19 is not of the second century of the sequence and is very possibly not of the lakebed at all. Consider: the amendment names its own interval. *Ninety years.* Nowhere else in thirty-one ostraka does a second hand date itself, because nowhere else does a second hand need to. The whole force of the convention is that the interval is felt and not stated. H19 states it. H19 states it and then, worse, *characterizes* it — "the whole authority of the far end" — a phrase which reads less like a Hesperine amendment than like a nineteenth-century essay *about* Hesperine amendment. It tells us what the form means. Genuine work does not do this. Genuine work simply is the thing, and lets Vaunel and Toresc fight about what it is.

I am aware that H19 is the fragment everyone loves. That is not an argument. It is a symptom.

**Toresc to the Editors:**

Vaunel has at last given us his method: *if it is good, it is fake.* One admires the economy.

Set aside the palaeography, which he sets aside — the incision depth, the tool profile, the salt crust that runs *over* the second hand's strokes on the verso and would have to have been counterfeited by a forger with access to a lakebed and ninety years to spare. Set it aside, because Vaunel's real claim is not evidential and cannot be answered with evidence. His claim is that the amendment is too articulate about its own condition.

But consider what he is proposing. He is proposing that a second hand which *understood what it was doing* is thereby disqualified. He wants his amenders unconscious. He wants them to have stumbled into the form the way water stumbles into a ditch. And I ask: on what grounds do we assume that a tradition of this refinement went four centuries without producing one practitioner willing to say aloud what the practice was for?

**Vaunel, in reply:**

Toresc has not read me, which is his custom, or has read me and preferred the version he can defeat.

I did not say self-awareness disqualifies. I said *this* self-awareness arrives in *this* idiom, and the idiom is ours. Grant me the crust. Grant me the tooling. Grant me every physical fact he likes. The forgery I am describing is not a forgery of clay.

And here is the part he will not touch, so I will hold it up. Suppose I am wrong. Suppose H19's second hand is as old as its salt. Then what have we got? A poem in which a man watches for nothing at the eighth hour, and ninety years later another man tells him he was right to watch. Toresc calls this the summit of the corpus. I call it the only fragment in which an amendment *comforts*. The other thirty do not comfort. They contradict, they complete, they turn the first hand inside out, and not one of them says *you were not wrong*. The consolation is the anomaly. The interval is not the anomaly.

So let him have his date. I withdraw nothing. If it is authentic, then some ancient amender broke the form by being kind in it, and we have spent a century mistaking a lapse for a masterpiece — and if it is not, then someone among our own great-grandfathers wanted very badly to be told that the watching counted, and made himself a voice from the far end to say so.

I no longer care which. Both are forgeries of the same thing. The clay is only where one of them happened.

**Toresc, final reply:**

Then we agree on the poem and disagree on the century, and Vaunel, who began by calling it false, ends by calling it unbearable.

I would only observe that he has now written three letters to the far end of a correspondence in which his opponent is obliged to answer, and complained the whole while that the arrangement is unfair.

## The gap

Islamic medicine, tenth through fourteenth centuries, had everything needed for this and didn't build it.

Ibn Sīnā's chapter on pulse in the *Canon* decomposes it into something close to ten independent dimensions: the size of the expansion in three axes, the force of the stroke, the speed of the movement, the duration of the rest between movements, the tension or laxity of the vessel wall, the fullness of the artery, and the regularity of the whole. He then names compound pulses after the things they feel like — gazelle, worm, ant, saw, mouse's tail, wave. Al-Rāzī, a century earlier, kept actual case notes (*Kitāb al-Tajārib*) tracking patients day by day. Paper was cheap from Samarqand and Baghdad. The clinical stakes were maximal: in fever, everything hung on periodicity and on the day of crisis.

So: a decomposed multidimensional variable, sampled repeatedly over days, whose *pattern across samples* is the diagnostic object, recorded by literate men with cheap paper — and it was all written in prose. "His pulse was small, weak, and rapid, and on the fourth day it became like the tail of a mouse." You cannot see a quartan rhythm in a paragraph.

Here is the notation they didn't build. Call it **khaṭṭ al-nabḍ**, the pulse-line; a sheet of it is a *waraqa*.

## Material constraints

**The pen.** A reed *qalam*, cut to a chisel nib, held one-handed. Rotating the wrist changes stroke width from hairline to full breadth *at no cost in time or ink*. This is the single most important economic fact about the medium, and the notation spends it on the most important clinical variable: force of the stroke. Strength is free.

**The ruling.** A *misṭara* — taut threads on card, pressed into dampened paper to emboss lines without ink. Ruling is reusable and free. But embossed lines are read by raking light and by finger, so you get *few reliable registers*, not many. Hence three: above the spine, on it, below it. Not a five-line staff. A physician's *misṭarat al-nabḍ* is a personal object; his apprentice inherits it.

**The hand.** The physician's fingers are on the wrist. He cannot write while feeling. Every glyph must be reconstructible from a few seconds of memory, immediately after lifting the hand. This forbids anything requiring precise measurement and forces the notation to be *gestural* — you write the shape of what you just felt.

**The clock.** There isn't one. Rate is counted against the physician's own respiration, as it actually was. So the notation has no absolute time axis: it has a **breath comb**, a tick above the spine at each of the physician's exhalations, and rate is read as beats-per-tooth. Practitioners call the making of it *tamshīṭ*, combing.

**Direction.** Right to left, on the embossed baseline, with marks above and below — because Arabic script already trains the eye to read a spine with supralinear and sublinear diacritics. I have to transcribe left-to-right below; that mirroring is a real loss, since in the original the illness runs into the page the way a sentence does.

## The system

**The spine is not zero. It is *this patient*.** On the first visit the physician writes the *aṣl*, the writ-of-health line: the pulse as this constitution's own norm. Every later line is read as departure from that. This is the theory baked into the notation, and it is straight Galenic–Avicennan doctrine: health is individual temperament, so there is no universal normal pulse to measure against. It will cost me later.

**Point marks** (per beat):
- One downstroke. **Width = force.** `▌` strong, `│` middling, `˙` a mere touch.
- **Height = size of expansion.** A stroke confined to the low register is small; one reaching the upper register is large.
- Strokes **joined** by a low sweep belong to one period; strokes **separated** by a lifted pen are discrete.

**Span marks** (above, over a stretch — because vessel texture is felt continuously, not per beat):
- `‾‾‾` hard, tense wall. `~~~` soft, lax.
- Nothing: unremarkable.

**Span marks** (below):
- `⌣⌣⌣` deep-lying; found only under pressure.
- A dot under a gap: rest notably prolonged.
- A *dotted* gap: **the hedge.** See below.

**Ideograms**: the named pulses, written as a single ligature of the animal's initial carried above the passage, replacing the strokes.

**Margin**: the day of illness, and a coarse sigil for the hour-quarter. Lines stack down the page, one per taking. That stacking is the whole point: periodicity becomes a shape.
