## Ambiguities it tolerates

Absolute rate — never recorded, because unrecordable and because deviation-from-own-breath was the operative quantity. Which wrist — the Galenic tradition took one and never asked. Skin heat, sweat, urine, sleep — recorded in prose alongside; the *waraqa* is a pulse instrument, not a chart. The exact ratio 3½ to the breath versus 3⅔ — the comb quantizes and nobody minded. Hour of day — four sigils, because "third hour" only had to be good enough to identify the paroxysm.

## Where it fights

**1. The ideogram eats the strokes.** Look at day 5. The gestalt names existed because *ẓaby* and *dūdī* are recognized faster than they are analyzed — the hand knows before the mind decomposes. So the ideogram is a span, and a span overwrites its interval. The result is that the notation's resolution is *inversely proportional to the strangeness of what it records*. Ordinary pulses get six parameters per beat; the pulse that decides the case gets one letter.

I did not design this. It fell out of committing to gestural writability plus a real lexicon, and it is the notation's central defect.

What the users would do: exactly what specialists always do. Apprentices' sheets are dense with strokes, because they can't yet see gazelles. Masters' sheets go sparse, and the sparseness becomes a display of authority — *I did not need to spell it out.* Then the arguments start: two physicians disagree at a bedside, and there is nothing in the record to arbitrate with, only two ligatures. Some *bīmāristān* imposes the double register — ideogram above, strokes below, write both — which doubles the labor and survives only in teaching, so that the manuscripts historians would later find are all pedagogical and all suspiciously thorough, and no one can tell from them how the thing was actually used.

**2. Absence and imperceptibility are the same gap.** A dropped beat and a beat too faint for the finger produce identical silence, and in a dying man the distinction is everything. The notation *must* write something, and a blank gap asserts too much. Hence the dotted gap: *I felt nothing and do not swear there was nothing.* It is the only hedge in the system, and it exists because omitting it was fatal.

Note what that implies. The system can express doubt about the patient's artery and has no mark at all for doubt about the finger — though rate is measured against a breath that quickens at a deathbed, and force against a memory of a baseline felt four days ago by a hand that was less tired. The instrument and the record share a body, and the notation cannot say so. A physician who wanted to say it would have to leave the notation and write a sentence in the margin, which is what the honest ones did, which is why the margins are where the interesting sentences are.

**3. And the fatal one: the spine is this patient.** Because every line is a departure from an individual writ-of-health, two *waraqas* cannot be compared. There is no aggregation, no series, no case-collection that adds up to a claim about tertian fevers in general. The notation is perfectly faithful to Galenic doctrine — health is particular temperament — and therefore generates no science. It would be a superb bedside instrument and would leave behind almost nothing worth copying, and the copies would be discarded with the patient, and that is the in-world explanation for why you have never heard of it.

Which is roughly the answer to why it never existed: a notation only survives if somebody has a reason to copy it. Staff notation survived because music is transmitted. Case notation isn't. The thing that made this notation good at its job is the thing that would have made it invisible to us.

**1. The kettle.**

The kettle stops. It does not end. There is a click, and the roar that had been building for ninety seconds falls out from under itself, and what's left is a different sound — the ticking of metal giving up heat, a few last bubbles detaching from the element and going up through water that is now merely very hot. Nothing about the boiling was completed. The kettle was not working toward anything. It was doing one thing at full commitment and then a bimetallic strip bent far enough to break a circuit, and the doing was over. If you flip the switch again it starts, and it is not resuming — there's no such thing as resuming a boil. It just does the same thing again from wherever the water happens to be.

**2. The sentence.**

A sentence ends. Even a bad one, even one that trails off — the trailing off is a way of ending, which is why we have a mark for it. What makes it an ending is that the sentence was going somewhere and the period is the place. You can hear this in the way a reader's voice drops on the last stressed syllable before a full stop, a drop that isn't there mid-clause. And a sentence can *also* stop, separately, which is how we know the two things aren't the same word: a sentence stops when the speaker is interrupted, or when the page is torn, and then it has stopped without ending, and the ear stays open, waiting, in a way it does not wait after a period. The waiting is the evidence.

**3. The glacier.**

Here it gets harder, and I want to be careful, because a glacier is exactly the kind of thing people use to mean something else, and I'm not doing that. A glacier is a river of ice that flows downhill at a few centimetres a day, and at the bottom it reaches a point where it melts as fast as it arrives, and that point is called the terminus. It is genuinely a *terminus*: the glacier ends there. Not because it accomplished anything, and not because it ran out — ice keeps arriving at the terminus forever, or for as long as there's ice — but because that's where the shape of the thing has its boundary. The end of a glacier is a place, and the place is maintained by continuous arrival. Whereas the glacier stops in a different sense, decades earlier, when the accumulation zone stops accumulating; and that stopping is invisible for a long time, and is happening now in most places, and doesn't move the terminus at all until it does.

So there's a thing that ends at a location while continuing, and stops in a way that takes forty years to show up at the location where it ends. I notice I want to say something here about how *stopping is about process and ending is about form* —

**4. The fever.**

A fever breaks. Not ends, not stops: breaks, which is a third word, and I don't know what to do with it. What happens physically is that the hypothalamic setpoint comes back down and the body, which is now above its own target, dumps heat — hence the sweat, which is the reason the person in the bed at four in the morning wakes soaked and clear-headed and knows something has happened without being told. The knowing is the strange part. The fever didn't reach a conclusion. Nothing in the fever pointed toward its own cessation the way a sentence points toward its period. And yet nobody says a fever stops, the way a kettle stops, because the person who had it experiences a shape: the climb, the plateau, the four bad nights, and then this. It has the felt structure of an ending laid over the mechanics of a stopping, and both descriptions are complete, and they don't contradict each other, and they don't merge.

**5. The record.**

The last track ends. Then there's the run-out groove, which is a spiral that goes nowhere, and the needle sits in it making a sound like a soft pulse once per revolution, and the record is still playing. It is playing nothing. It will play nothing for as long as the motor turns. And the person in the chair has to get up.

## From *A Lexicon of Unwitnessed Things*

---

### **antelection** *n.* /ˌantɪˈlɛkʃən/

**Etym.** Latin *ante-* "before" + *lectiō* "a reading, a gathering-up," on the model of *predilection*; first proposed by analogy with the printer's term *fore-edge*.

**Def.** The peripheral pre-apprehension of a sentence one has not yet read: its length, the position of its commas, the mass and probable stress of its final word — absorbed as shape rather than sense, and used to set the pace and expectation of the reading that follows. Antelection governs the reader's tempo continuously and can be demonstrated by its consequences (the stumble at an unexpectedly long clause), but it terminates the instant attention is directed at it, at which point the reader is merely looking ahead at words, which is a different and coarser act.

**Ex.** *(clinical)* "Gaze-contingent masking of the parafoveal field abolished antelection without impairing lexical access, though subjects reported the text had become 'effortful' or 'stepwise.'"

**Ex.** *(intimate)* "I could tell from across the page that the paragraph ended badly — the last line was short, and short lines are where people put the deaths — and I slowed down before I knew why."

**Lexicographer's note.** Antelection belongs to the class of phenomena whose only witness is also their solvent. Introspection is the wrong instrument here, not because the phenomenon is faint but because attention is precisely the thing it operates in the absence of; to look for it is to replace it with a competent imitation. Languages name what can be pointed at, and antelection cannot be pointed at from within. It had to wait not for a word but for an apparatus — for someone to think of stealing the edge of the page away and watching the reader falter.

---

### **anecdysis** *n.* /anɪkˈdʌɪsɪs/

**Etym.** Greek *anékdota* "things unpublished, private stories" + *ékdysis* "a shedding, a stripping off." The overlap of the two roots at *-ekd-* is coincidental and has been called (by the compilers) undeserved good fortune.

**Def.** The slow, unremarked turnover of the small repertoire of stories by which a person represents themselves to others, such that over a period of roughly seven to fifteen years the entire set is replaced without a single deliberate retirement. Each story ceases to be told slightly before it ceases to be true of the teller; each new story enters the repertoire already smoothed, as though it had always been there. No episode of anecdysis has ever been observed at the moment of its occurrence, since it consists of nothing happening on any particular occasion.

**Ex.** *(clinical)* "Longitudinal transcripts of the same eleven subjects at four intervals showed near-total substitution of self-descriptive narrative units, with no subject able to date the disappearance of any unit and four subjects denying the prior existence of units they had themselves supplied verbatim in earlier sessions."

**Ex.** *(intimate)* "He told the one about the boat again and I realised I hadn't heard the one about his father and the ladder for years, and that I couldn't ask for it, because asking would make it a specimen."

**Lexicographer's note.** This phenomenon resisted naming for the ordinary reason that it has no instants. Vocabulary accretes around events — thresholds, ruptures, the nameable minute — and anecdysis offers none; it is composed entirely of omissions, and omissions leave no mark in the medium where they occur. It is also, uncomfortably, easier for others to observe than for oneself, and words for things visible chiefly to spouses and siblings tend not to be coined, being unnecessary between people who can simply glance at each other instead.

---

### **koinosigy** *n.* /kɔɪˈnɒsɪdʒi/

**Etym.** Greek *koinós* "common, held jointly" + *sigḗ* "silence." Compare the legal Latin *res nullius*, a thing belonging to no one.

**Def.** A silence maintained by two or more people, each of whom would prefer it broken, and each of whom preserves it out of deference to a preference falsely attributed to the others. Koinosigy is not shyness, which is individual, nor companionable quiet, which is wanted; it is a structure that no participant authors, sustained by the sum of their courtesies. It has no interior: each person experiences only their own restraint and the apparent composure of everyone else. It ends without residue the moment anyone speaks, and cannot be recovered afterward, since all parties will report having been about to.

**Ex.** *(clinical)* "Post-hoc questionnaires indicated that in 84% of trials the silence was disvalued by every member of the dyad, a divergence between private preference and inferred group norm consistent with pluralistic ignorance."

**Ex.** *(intimate)* "Nine floors of it, and then the doors opened and we both said something at once, in the corridor, where it was allowed."

**Lexicographer's note.** The obstacle here is neither speed nor slowness but ownership. Koinosigy is real and yet is not any person's experience; it exists only in the aggregate, and aggregates have no tongues. Every first-person account of it is necessarily a misdescription — "I was too polite to speak" is a report of a fragment mistaken for the whole — and languages are built almost entirely out of first-person accounts. What was needed was not a subtler observer but a second one, comparing notes; the phenomenon becomes visible only in the moment two people admit, afterward, to having wanted the same thing and each having declined it on the other's behalf. It is likely that most of the unnamed is like this: not too small to see, but held in common, and therefore held by nobody.

**On forward commitment in function words, with notes on the asymmetry of debt**

The property I want to describe is how much of a sentence's future a word has already spent.

Consider *but* and *nevertheless*. The standard account distinguishes them by register and by strength of contrast, which is true and uninteresting. The difference that organizes them is this: after *but*, almost anything can occur. After *nevertheless*, the number of continuations that will not fail has collapsed by some large factor. *Nevertheless* has committed to a concessive relation whose second term must be a full independent clause, must assert rather than ask, must be in some relation of surprise to what preceded, and must not itself introduce a further concession without producing a sentence that no one will finish. *But* has committed to almost nothing. It can be followed by a clause, a fragment, a single word, a question, a repetition, silence.

The same relation holds for *and* / *moreover*, *so* / *accordingly*, *though* / *albeit*, *also* / *furthermore*. In each pair the longer member has mortgaged more. This correlates with syllable count often enough to look causal, and I don't think it is causal — I think both are downstream of how often the word is used, since a word used constantly cannot afford to constrain its environment much.

There is a class of words whose entire function is to incur an enforceable debt. *Not only* obligates a later *but also*, or a licensed substitute. *Either* obligates *or*. *Both* obligates *and*. *So* in one of its uses obligates *that*. What distinguishes these from ordinary selectional requirements is that the debt has a due date, and there is a determinate point past which it can no longer be discharged — not a point of ungrammaticality exactly, but a point after which paying it produces something worse than never having promised. A sentence that opens *not only* and runs long enough will eventually pass out of the range in which the second term can arrive at all, and what happens then is that the speaker restructures backward and pretends the promise was never made. This is the default outcome in speech rather than the exception. The obligation is real and almost always defaulted on.

The asymmetry: no word obligates anything *before* it. There is no morpheme in English which, appearing at position n, requires that position n−4 have been a particular thing. All syntactic debt runs forward.

The apparent counterexamples are instructive because they all turn out to bind to something other than syntax. *Respectively* is the strongest case — it is a function applied retroactively to text already committed, an instruction to return to two earlier enumerations and pair them index by index, and it fails if the earlier enumerations differ in cardinality. But what it requires is not a *word*; it requires that the preceding material have a certain arithmetic property. *The former* requires a prior antecedent — again a property of the discourse, not a licensed lexical item. *Too* and *either* in negative-polarity use (*I don't either*) require a prior negation, and that negation may have been produced by a different speaker on a different day. *Again* requires that the event have occurred before, which is a fact about the world.

So the rule holds in the strong form: forward-binding words bind to syntax; backward-binding words bind to the world or to the record. Grammar can promise and cannot demand.

A related specimen, differently constructed: the words whose meaning is entirely their position. *Only*, *just*, *even*, *merely*. These do not have a meaning that then gets located somewhere in the sentence; they are operators taking whatever is adjacent as argument, and the same four phonemes will produce seven mutually inconsistent claims depending on where they are inserted into a six-word clause. Speakers place them by a rule they cannot state and hearers recover the intended argument by a rule they also cannot state, and the recovery is not always the placement, which is why *only* is the most frequent source of unintended assertion in written English. It is a word with no content and enormous consequence, which puts it in a very small family.

And on questions, since you asked about their shapes: a question is a hole with a declared arity and a declared type. *Who* declares arity one and type person. *When* declares arity one and type interval-or-instant. *Why* declares neither. It does not specify how many answers would fill it, or at what level of the causal structure the answer should be taken from, or whether a mechanism or a purpose or a history is wanted. This is why a *why* question can receive a true answer and remain open. It is not discharged by correctness. It is discharged by acceptance, which is a property of the asker rather than the answer, and which means *why* is the only interrogative whose satisfaction condition is not in the sentence.

One last specimen, and I'll stop where the description stops.

*Notwithstanding* is, as far as I can determine, nearly alone in English in being able to precede or follow its own object with no change in meaning and almost none in register. *Notwithstanding these facts.* *These facts notwithstanding.* Nothing else common does this. *Ago* has committed to the second position only and cannot occupy the first. *Aside* likewise. Prepositions in general have committed to the first position so thoroughly that the exceptions are archaisms and legal formulae. *Notwithstanding* is a preposition that has declined to specify which side of its argument it stands on, and it has survived in this condition for something like six hundred years without either variant becoming the marked one.

# NOTES

*Vaughan, S. E., "Before the Water" (1936). NLW MS 24,118B. Edited with notes by Idris Pugh.*

---

**1.** The MS is a single fair copy in soft pencil, 72 lines in nine stanzas of eight, written on the versos of four Board of Education inspection forms bearing the printed heading NANTWYN BOARD SCHOOL and the date 1936. It is untitled. I have taken the title from her letter to Alice Trewin of 14 October 1936 ("I have written the thing at last, my poem from before the water"), and I take responsibility for it. The MS was recovered in 1954 from a trunk at Ty'n-y-Coed and is water-stained across the lower third of the first sheet. Reviewers have remarked on the irony at tedious length. I would rather they remarked on the poem.

**2.** l. 1, *the road going down* — The parish road descended from the Llanfair turning through three-quarters of a mile of limes, planted by the Cathrall estate in the 1840s and felled by the Corporation in the spring of 1937. The poem's occasion is her last walk down it: she was in the valley from 28 September to 4 October 1936, and the valve-house was closed on the 11th. She stood, as I did, on ground that now lies under some sixty feet of water.

**3.** l. 4, *seventeen years* — She left Nantwyn in the summer of 1919, aged twenty-two, and did not return in her father's lifetime. Neither the letters nor the two surviving notebooks account for this. It is not for me to speculate on a family quarrel at sixty years' distance, and I shall not.

**4.** l. 7, *the bees still at it in the lime* — Limes flower in June. The poem is set unmistakably in the first week of October. I take this for licence rather than error: she is hearing the avenue as it was, not as it stood. Those who wish to correct her are welcome to try to improve the line.

**5.** ll. 9–12 — The schoolroom. The door-frame of the infants' room was marked in chalk each Michaelmas with the children's heights, and the marks were not washed off; her line about "the little ladder of them going up the jamb" is exact. My own mark was there, at three feet eleven, with Gwilym Preece's above it and Nansi Hughes's above his. I have never read these four lines without difficulty.

**6.** l. 14, *the smell of the whitewash going over* — The Corporation whitewashed the interiors of all eleven dwellings and both outbuildings before demolition, for reasons of sanitation. The smell of wet lime is the smell of that autumn, and she has it right.

**7.** l. 16, *the tongue stopped at last* — The chapel bell (Rudhall, 1782) was taken down on 1 October, bedded in straw in a farm cart, and removed to Llanfair-ar-y-Bryn, where it hangs. I saw it go. "At last" is the exhaustion of a long grief speaking; the phrase should not be pressed further than that.

**8.** ll. 17–24 — The graveyard. Twenty-two interments were lifted and reburied at Llanfair between 21 September and 2 October; my uncle Tom Preece was one of the bearers. Among them was Evan Vaughan of Tŷ Isaf, deacon and tenant farmer, the poet's father, who died in November 1931. She had not attended his funeral — illness, I think we must assume, though she says nothing of it — and so she came, five years late, to see him carried up the hill. This is the still centre of the poem and the reason she made the journey.

**9.** ll. 22–23 — The water-stain. Three words, possibly four, are lost from the end of 22 and the beginning of 23, in the passage where the coffin is brought up out of the ground. Of the first lost word there survives a lower loop and the start of an ascender, giving *gl-*. I read *gloom*, which suits the sense and the season. Dr Menna Rhys, in her essay "A Poem of Deliverance" (*Planet*, 1989), reads *glad*, and builds upon that single mutilated syllable a case for the whole poem which I can only call wilfully perverse. She was not born in the valley. She did not stand in that field.

**10.** l. 26, *his boots by the door still the shape of him* — Left where they were for five years by the tenant who followed. A detail of great tenderness, and characteristic: she will not say *father* anywhere in the poem, but she will look at his boots.

**11.** l. 28, *the strap on its nail behind the door* — A harness strap. Tŷ Isaf kept two horses until 1929. Farm gear appears throughout her work as a kind of shorthand for the life she left, and the nail is remembered as precisely as the boots.

**12.** ll. 33–40 — The locking of the house. "The door that was never locked in his lifetime; / I locked it, and put the key in the river." No key was required of departing tenants; the act is her own invention and entirely ritual, an elegiac gesture of closure such as the folk practice of the region offers many parallels for. Cf. the turning of a mirror to the wall.

**13.** l. 41, *the new horizon, painted round the hills* — The Corporation's surveyors marked the top water level with a band of red lead on trees and rock faces around the whole circuit of the valley, so that all summer one could see exactly where the water would come to and walk about beneath it. The resident engineer was H. J. Corfield, MICE, whose name is misgiven as Cofield in every account but this one.

**14.** l. 44, *the pump going all night, and the hot oil smell of it* — Strictly a compressor, at the cut-off trench. But nobody in the valley called it anything but the pump, and I have let her have it.

**15.** ll. 49–52 — The orchard at Tŷ Isaf; the trout "standing" in the shallow of the Nant Wen; the sheep hurdles stacked for the sale. All of this went under. The apple was a Pig's Nose Pippin, a local sort, of which cuttings survive at Llanfair vicarage.

**16.** l. 51 — A tear in the sheet, with slight scorching at the edge, has taken one word of two syllables from the middle of the line. She smoked incessantly and carelessly all her life. I have left the gap open. I have been urged to fill it and I will not.

**17.** ll. 53–56 — She quotes the hymn "Trwy'r dyfroedd dyfnion" — *through the deep waters* — and gets it wrong, giving *o'r* for *trwy'r*, **out of** the deep waters for **through** them. Her Welsh, always the second language of the household, had rusted badly in Shropshire, and the slip is understandable; I record it only for completeness.

**18.** l. 60, *the water coming up like sleep on a stair* — The finest line she wrote, and I have said so in print before (see my "The Nantwyn Poems," *Anglo-Welsh Review*, 1971). Note that the simile is not of drowning but of arrival: something long expected coming up through a house at the end of a day. Even here, in the deepest of her grief, the craftsmanship holds.

**19.** l. 68 — The MS plainly reads *loosed*: "and the whole of it loosed from me." This is a slip of the pencil for *lost*, which the sense demands and which I have printed, with the MS reading recorded here so that no one may accuse me of tidying her. She wrote fast, in a farm kitchen, on the back of a school form, with the cart coming in the morning. She was not correcting proofs.

**20.** l. 72 — The final word is gone: the corner of the fourth sheet is torn away cleanly, as though on a fold. Line 71 ends *cease*, and the stanzas close in couplets throughout, so that the rhyme is fixed and the choice of word ought to be narrow. I have supplied *grief* — unrhymed, and I know it — because I believe that at the last, with the water twelve days off, she let the form go, and that the broken rhyme is the point. Against this must be set a pencilled word in the margin of the MS, in Alice Trewin's small upright hand: *release*. Miss Trewin came into her life in 1943, seven years after the valley closed, knew nothing of Nantwyn, and had a lifelong taste for consolation; her interpolation is sentimental and I reject it.

I have worked on this poem for forty-one years. It is very nearly all that is left of the place where I was born, and it is a poem of mourning, whatever is now fashionable to say of it; I have named my daughter for the woman who wrote it. If I have been wrong anywhere, it is not for want of love.

*I. P., Wrexham, 1994*

## The Kessock Nineteen: A History of the Order Question

### I. The loss

The box came out of a field above the Kessock narrows in the spring of 1847, turned up by a tenant named John Mowat while he was clearing what he took to be a stone. He wrote to his minister that he had found "ane auld kist, and in it nine and ten wee bodies of wood, ilk ane different." The phrasing matters, because it is the only independent attestation of the count, and it is a count made by a man holding a lamp over a box he had just prised open.

The kist travelled to Edinburgh three weeks later and fell from the tail of a cart at the foot of Leith Walk. The outer box survived; what did not survive was the bed — a thin laminated tray of pine, fitted with nineteen shallow recesses, which split along the grain and shed most of its lamination into the mud. Seven fragments were recovered, representing something between thirty-eight and forty-four per cent of the original bed, depending on whose reconstruction of the perimeter you accept. The objects themselves were gathered up by two porters and a boy.

In 1889 one of the porters, then seventy-one, told an interviewer that three of the "wee wooden men" had been "put by" overnight and handed in the following day. No one has ever been able to decide whether this is testimony or embroidery, and the whole subsequent literature is haunted by it, because every reconstruction of the arrangement requires the assemblage to be closed at nineteen.

The objects were accessioned by a clerk who laid them out left to right as they came out of a bag and numbered them I–XIX. This arbitrary sequence has poisoned everything since.

### II. The Ordinalists

The sequence school begins properly with Hew Dalrymple Gair's paper of 1901, and its foundation is not textual at all but arboreal. Gair established — by grain, by ray-fleck, by the drift of a single resin canal across successive pieces — that eighteen of the nineteen objects were cut from one billet of yew, and that they could be arranged in an unbroken series in which the grain of each object continues into the next. Eighteen consecutive slices. The series is not a hypothesis; you can see it, and it has never been seriously challenged.

From this Gair argued the obvious: an order was already given in the material, and a maker who troubled to carve nineteen dissimilar objects from one billet in sequence and then cut nineteen fitted recesses to hold them was very unlikely to have shuffled them at the last moment. The arrangement, therefore, is the carving order or its reverse, and the Order Question is answered.

The textual buttress arrived later and did the school more harm than good. It is a marginal note in a 1602 Inverness notarial protocol book, in a lawyer's hand, reading *the nyntene of Kessok, quhilk mon be tauld in ordour*. The Ordinalists took *tauld in ordour* as decisive — counted in order, therefore ordered, therefore sequential. Their opponents pointed out, correctly and often, that nobody has ever shown the note refers to these objects, that "Kessok" is a common enough place-name element, and that the note may be about tenants. Gair's successors kept citing it anyway, and the sense that the school was propping up strong physical evidence with a bad scrap of paper cost it credibility it did not need to lose.

The Ordinalists' real weakness is subtler. Twelve of the nineteen objects carry incised tallies on their undersides: short strokes, one to seven of them, in no arrangement anyone can reconcile with the grain series. Gair proposed that the tallies were a maker's aid and had been cut before the objects were finally sized, hence their disorder. This is not impossible. It is also not an argument.

### III. The Morphologists

Andrew Bervie Lauder's position, developed at Glasgow from about 1908, was that "order" was a category error. The bed was a two-dimensional field. A field has no first and no last. What could be recovered was a *layout*, and it could be recovered without recourse to a single document, by treating the seven tray fragments and the objects as a constraint-satisfaction problem: each object has a footprint, each surviving recess has an outline, and the recesses are shallow and close-fitted enough that most objects will only sit in one or two of them.

This was genuinely powerful work. Lauder's group added the resin evidence — the bed had been coated, and each recess retains a stain-ring of measurable depth where an object rested — and by the 1930s they had four recesses assigned to specific objects with something close to certainty, and a reconstructed perimeter that constrained the missing area to a strip along one long side. The Morphologists were doing archaeology; the Ordinalists, increasingly, were doing philology at things.

Their weakness was arithmetic. The reconstructed bed, extrapolated from the perimeter and the fragment curvature, has room for eighteen recesses. To get nineteen, Lauder's successors had to assume a narrower gutter than any surviving fragment shows.

### IV. The plates

The two schools would have argued anyway. What made the argument permanent was Lauder's 1913 folio of photographic plates, which remains the standard visual record.

Lauder photographed the objects in his own proposed layout. He did not label it as a reconstruction. He captioned the objects by plate and figure — Plate 2, fig. c — and within a decade every student in Britain knew the Kessock objects by Lauder's designations, which encoded his layout, in an order that had no authority whatsoever and looked, on the page, exactly like a fact. Gair called it "the great smuggling," and he was not wrong. From 1913 until the concordance of 1961, to cite an object at all you had to choose a numbering system, and the choice announced your allegiance before you had made a single claim. There is no more effective way to harden a disagreement than to make the notation partisan.

The personal wound was smaller and worse. Gair and Lauder had shared rooms as students; Gair had supplied, over four years and unpublished, the caliper measurements that appear uncredited in the plate captions; the acknowledgement reads "with thanks to the staff of the Museum." Gair never published on Kessock again after 1919. He did, however, referee.

## 1. The tuning fork

Every other item on this list is one thing. The tuning fork is two things forced to pretend they are one. It has two tines, and its whole trick depends on them moving in opposite directions at once — apart, together, apart — a quarrel so fast and so regular that we mistake it for a single clear voice. Nothing else here is built out of its own disagreement. The list is a list of unities. The fork is a marriage.

## 2. The cul-de-sac

Every dead end on this list is permanent. The tooth does not go back in. The language does not come back. The ice does not un-melt, the word does not un-split, the twist cannot be undone without cutting. These are all terminal facts.

The cul-de-sac is a dead end you can leave. You arrive at the end of it, you go around the little circle — and that circle is the point, it exists so that nothing has to reverse, nothing has to be undone, no mistake has to be admitted — and then you drive back out onto the road you came in on, and nothing has happened to you. It is the only ending here that costs nothing. A dead end with a turning circle is not a dead end. It is an errand.

## 3. The sourdough starter

Use a tuning fork and you have not diminished it. Walk down the cul-de-sac, count to six, look at the Möbius strip, read by the lighthouse, wedge the door, hold the tooth in your palm, ask the old woman to say the word for *rain* — none of these are spent. They are all there afterward, entire.

The starter is the only item on this list that you must destroy a portion of in order to consult. Every loaf is an amputation. You reach into the jar and take out something that will never come back, and then you feed what remains so that it can grow enough to be robbed again next week. That is not use. That is husbandry, and it is a different relationship entirely from the one you have with the other ten.

## 4. The number 6

Ten of these things are maintenance problems.

The fork goes flat; steel creeps, temperature bends the pitch, and someone has to check it against something truer. The cul-de-sac cracks and heaves and must be resurfaced by a municipality that would rather not. The starter starves in a week. Antarctica is losing itself into the sea at a rate we now measure in gigatons per year. *Cleave* is drifting — the "cling" sense is dying, and holding it in the language takes deliberate literary effort. The tooth yellows in the drawer. The paper strip tears at the seam. The lighthouse rusts, salt-eaten, and the state either pays or lets it fall. The last speaker is eighty-nine. The doorstop wears down at the toe.

Every one of those is a battle with entropy that someone, somewhere, is currently losing. The number 6 is the sum of its own divisors, it was that in the Cambrian, it will be that after the last star, and no one has to do anything about it. It is the only item here that is not being kept alive.

## 5. Antarctica

Ten of these are cultural objects. Not merely useful, not merely noticed — *invented*.

Someone set A440 by committee. Someone platted the cul-de-sac, and someone else wrote the zoning code that made it profitable. The starter is a domesticated ecology, a herd. Six is a concept with a history. *Cleave* is two Old English verbs, *clēofan* and *clifian*, that human mouths wore into each other. The shed tooth is nothing without the drawer, the envelope, the coin under the pillow — biology sheds it, culture *keeps* it, and it is the keeping that puts it on this list. Möbius described his strip in 1858; before that it was not a thing, it was a possibility. The lighthouse is a public work. The "last fluent speaker" is a designation conferred by a discipline; it is a linguist's category before it is a person's condition. The doorstop is a solution to a problem that only exists because we built hinges.

Antarctica was there. It would be exactly what it is — the same wind off the same plateau, the same two miles of ice sitting on the same buried mountains — if hominids had never happened. It is the only item on this list that is not about us.

## 6. The word *cleave*

Earlier I said the tuning fork was two things pretending to be one. That was a small observation about a small object, and it was wrong about which item it described.

*Cleave* means to split and it means to cling. These are not two shades of one idea; they are opposites, and they are not even related. Two separate verbs with two separate ancestries collapsed into one spelling by accident of sound change. Nothing is holding them together but the shape of the word. Every other item here is a single thing that *appears* to have two aspects — the lighthouse warns and welcomes, the tooth is loss and growth, the doorstop opens and closes, and in every case one thing is doing two jobs. *Cleave* is not one thing doing two jobs. It is two things wearing one body, unrelated, non-communicating, permanently mistaken for each other.

Everything else on this list has an identity. *Cleave* has a coincidence.

## 7. The shed baby tooth

Go down the list and ask what each thing is doing right now.

The fork is ready to be struck. The cul-de-sac is turning a delivery van around. The starter is rising. Six is summing to itself. Antarctica is freezing. *Cleave* is being used, badly, in a sermon. The strip is running its single surface under someone's finger. The lighthouse is lit. The speaker is speaking. The doorstop is holding a door.

The tooth is finished. Its work is entirely over — it chewed for six years and was evicted by its successor, which is the only career it ever had and it completed it. Every other item on this list is in the middle of something. The tooth is retired, and worse, it has been kept: it has passed out of the world of function into the world of relics, where things exist purely to be evidence. It is the only item here in the past tense.

## 8. The Möbius strip

Now look at what the list is actually made of. It is made of two-sidedness.

The fork's two tines. The cul-de-sac's in and out. The starter fed or starved. Six as sum and as product of its factors. Antarctica's six months of light and six of dark. *Cleave*'s split and cling. The tooth's loss and growth. The lighthouse's beam and dark arc, sea and shore, come-in and stay-away. The last speaker, who has a language on one side of her and no one on the other. The doorstop's open and shut.

Eleven items, and ten of them are hinged. The Möbius strip is the one object in human hands with a single side — draw the line and it comes back to itself having covered everything, no inside, no outside, no other face to turn to. It is not merely different from the other ten. It is their negation. The list is a wall of doors, and the strip is the one surface with nowhere else to be.

## 9. The lighthouse

Every item on this list is a form of holding on.

The fork holds a pitch. The cul-de-sac holds cars, keeps them from passing through, and holds a certain kind of quiet for the people who paid for it. The starter holds a lineage — some of them a hundred years of unbroken continuity, the oldest surviving domesticated thing in most kitchens. Six holds itself: it is perfect, its parts add back up to exactly what they came from, a number that does not leak. Antarctica holds the record — eight hundred thousand years of atmosphere in a column of ice, the planet's only intact memory. *Cleave* holds two dead verbs, and half of what it means is literally *to cling*. The tooth is held; that is its entire remaining purpose. The strip holds a twist and cannot be talked out of it. The last speaker holds a language against the whole weight of a century. The doorstop holds a door.

The lighthouse pushes away. Its message is *not here*, *not this way*, *turn*. It is the one item on this list whose function is to keep something from arriving. And it does this for strangers, in the dark, whom it will never meet and cannot see, and if it succeeds nothing happens and no one thanks it. Ten items are grips. One is a hand held up.

## 10. The last fluent speaker of a language

Ten of these things do not mind.

That is the asymmetry, and it is so large that everything above was a rounding error. The fork does not mind being flat. Antarctica does not mind. The starter, which is alive, does not mind starving; it has no position on the matter. Six has no interior. The lighthouse does not experience the dark, and the tooth does not miss the mouth, and the word *cleave* is not embarrassed.

The last fluent speaker of a language is the only item on this list for which *being on this list* is a thing that is undergone. She knows. That is the whole content of the category — you cannot be the last speaker without the knowledge, or you are just an old woman. She has a hundred thousand words that arrive in her mouth with nowhere to go, jokes that cannot land, a word for a bird that stopped existing, and the specific loneliness of being the only room a language has left. She is not a thing that means something. She is someone to whom something is happening.

Ten objects and one grief. That is the odd one out, and it is not close.

## 11. The doorstop

Except that she can hold a door.

That is the sentence that ends this. Because the last speaker can hold a door open, and so can the tuning fork, and the tooth, and the jar of starter, and the strip of paper folded enough times, and a stone brought back from Antarctica, and a dictionary open to *cleave*, and the little brass plaque off a decommissioned lighthouse. Nine of these things can be a doorstop by tomorrow morning. The doorstop cannot be any of them, ever, by any effort at all.

That is not a difference of degree. It means the doorstop is not on the list. Every other entry names a thing — a particular, an object or a place or a person or a number, something with an identity that cannot be handed off. Antarctica cannot be understudied. Six cannot send a substitute. The last speaker is irreplaceable in the strongest sense available to the word: replacing her is precisely the thing that cannot be done. *Cleave* is not a job that some other word could take a turn at.

A doorstop is a job. It is a role, a vacancy, a shape of need in a hallway, and it is filled at random by whatever was nearest — a brick, a shoe, a folded receipt, a fire extinguisher, a sleeping dog. Nothing is a doorstop; things are *doing* doorstop, briefly, and then they quit and go back to being bricks. The word is a verb in a noun's coat. Ten members of this list are things that are what they are. The eleventh is an opening that things fall into.

Which is why the answer was always going to be the doorstop, and why the other ten arguments had to be made first, and why they were all true and none of them mattered. ## The keeper of the blue vat

**What it was.** In any woollen town with a dyehouse, one man in the shop did nothing but keep the indigo vats alive. Everyone else dipped, wrung, hung, carted. He fed. A woad or indigo vat does not dissolve its dye — indigo is insoluble, and the only way to get it into cloth is to persuade a warm alkaline broth to eat the oxygen out of it, at which point it goes yellow-green and soluble and will strike into wool, and the blue only appears afterwards, in the air, on the drying pole. The eating was done by bacteria living in bran and madder and couched woad, in about three hundred gallons of liquor held at roughly blood heat in a brick-set copper sunk to its rim in the floor. That colony had to be kept hungry but not starving, sweet but not sour, hot but not cooked. It could be killed in an afternoon by a careless assistant and it took nine days to raise a new one. So: one man, permanently, for the vats.

**Tools.** A larch pole with an oak cross pegged to the end, for "rousing" — a slow figure-eight from the shoulders that turned the liquor without breaking the film on top. A long-shafted pewter dipper, shallow as a saucer, for lifting a sample without drowning the flower. A horn cup. A notched hazel rod for sounding the sediment, so he knew how much dead matter lay on the bottom and how much room was left before the vat had to be emptied and re-set. An iron ladle for lime. A flue-door and a coal shovel, and a boy.

And the hanks. A nail-board along the wall of the vat house carrying skeins of white worsted, each one dipped for a single count and hung, in order, from the vat's first morning to its last. Twenty, thirty hanks per vat, palest at the left. That was the instrument. No thermometer worth trusting, no hydrometer, no colour standard — instead, a physical ledger of what this particular copper had done on each of its days, so that today's dip could be held against the eleventh day of the last three vats and judged.

**The competence.** Reading the flower. A working vat carries a scum — coppery, bronze-shot, veined blue where the liquor breaks through. The colour of it, the size of the cells, the way the film healed after the pole went through, the width of the dark ring at the rim: these told you whether the vat wanted feeding, sweetening, or leaving alone. Then the taste. He took a horn cup off the dipper and held it against his palate, and what he was tasting was free alkali against the sourness of fermentation — too sharp and it wanted bran, too soapy and slick and it had been over-limed and would go dun and refuse to strike. A shopful of men could describe the taste. Two or three in a county could act on it correctly within an hour.

The ten years went not into learning this but into learning *vats* — because the reading is local. Water, bricks, the draught in that particular building, the bran from that particular mill, all of it makes a vat with its own mouth. A man who had kept the same four coppers for a decade could be brought forty miles to a strange dyehouse and be no better than an apprentice there for a year. This is the part that never got written down, and could not have been.

Below the tasting, one more thing: the count. Depth of shade was got by repeated short dips with an airing between, and there was no test but the eye on a wet greenish cloth that had not yet become blue. He called the number of dips for a customer's pattern, in advance, off the hank board, and was wrong perhaps once a season.

**The year.** The vat house did not run on the calendar; it ran on cloth. But the weather ran the vat. Hard frost was the enemy — the sunk copper leaked heat into the floor all night, the ferment slowed and sulked, and the keeper slept in the vat house on a board with the flue cracked open, up twice to rouse. Late July and August were worse in a different way: heat took a vat from sweet to stinking sour in six hours, and August is exactly when broadcloth had to be finished for autumn markets. The two bad seasons therefore both fell on him personally, and the man who kept the vats was, by trade custom, not expected to be at his own harvest, his own hay, or anybody's wedding in August.

**What it did to them.** Blue in the knuckle creases and under the nails, permanently, and everyone knows that part. Beyond it: forearms hairless and shiny to above the elbow, the skin thinned and shining from years of lime and heat, cracking every winter. Fingertips worn smooth — he judged temperature by hand and slime by finger, in and out of hot liquor forty times a day. The front teeth went first, the upper incisors, glassy at the edges and then chipping away, from tasting alkali several times daily for thirty years; and the molars stayed sound, which is how you tell a vat keeper's skull. A chronic cough from the ammonia coming off a vat in flower, in a hot wet unventilated house. And the stoop, which was not the general labourer's stoop: he worked bent from the hips with both arms in to the elbow over a rim at knee height, so the ruin was low back and the fronts of the shoulders, and old ones stood with the upper arms rolled permanently forward, as though still reaching into something.

**What killed it.** Two things, seven years apart. In 1897 synthetic indigo arrived in commercial quantity — pure, weighable, identical from drum to drum, which removed the need to judge strength from the raw material. That alone did not do it; you still had to reduce it, and reduction still meant a ferment. Then in 1904, sodium hydrosulphite came to market. It reduces indigo chemically, cold or warm, in minutes, in a vat with nothing alive in it. You weigh indigo, you weigh caustic, you weigh hydrosulphite, you check with a paper strip and a printed card, and a man can be taught it in a fortnight. The vat has no flower, no mouth, no bad August, no ninth day. It cannot be starved or soured. It also cannot be read, because there is nothing in it that changes on its own.

The keepers were kept on. That is the documented part: houses that converted between 1905 and 1912 retained their vat men, at wage, out of straightforward nervousness — and then found there was nothing for them to attend to. Some were made foremen. Some went to the drying floors.

**Why there is no word for the hole.** Because "dyer" survived. The word came through unharmed, still in use, still meaning a man who colours cloth for money, and the specific ten-year competence it had contained for four hundred years fell out of the inside of it without leaving any mark on the outside. So there was never a moment when anyone needed a new term for an absence, or noticed one.

The hank boards were the last to go. They stayed nailed up in converted vat houses for decades, because nobody's job it was to take them down: rows of little white-to-navy skeins gone grey with dust, in strict order, unlabelled, and by 1930 no one in the building could say what they had been for.

# ENCYCLOPAEDIA OF THE NINTH SHORE

*Being a Compendium of Matters Domestic, Natural, and Antiquarian. Fourth Edition, Revised.*

---

**BED-ICE, PERPETUAL.** The ice that lies upon the floors of the deeper sounds, lochs, and ocean basins, and which is not observed to diminish in summer. Its thickness in the Trennick Deep was sounded at nine fathoms by the *Pelican* survey (1874) and at nine fathoms and a hand by the *Pelican* survey repeated (1891), a discrepancy which has occasioned more literature than it deserves.

The question in dispute is whether the bed-ice of the great basins is annually renewed — that is, laid down each winter and wasted each summer in near-perfect balance — or whether it is a body of great antiquity, to which each winter adds a film so thin as to escape measurement. Professor Vestergaard has argued the former with characteristic vigour and admirable clarity, and it would be presumptuous of the present compiler to suppose that so eminent an authority could be mistaken in any matter of principle. It is nevertheless worth remarking, in the humblest spirit, that the core drawn from the Trennick floor by Dr. Halloran contained, at a depth of seven fathoms, the intact carcase of a *Delphinus* of a species not recorded living within the memory of the trade, together with a quantity of volcanic ash corresponding to no eruption in the parish registers. Professor Vestergaard has replied, with the courtesy for which he is justly celebrated, that the core may have been mislabelled. Dr. Halloran has responded that this is entirely possible, and that he would welcome the Professor's assistance in relabelling it. The correspondence continues, to the great edification of all.

*See* FLOOR OF THE DEEP; CLEAR, THE; SHOVE, THE.

---

**CARRIER, FISH-.** A licensed itinerant, formerly of the northern parishes, whose office was to remove the stock of shallow waters before the hard of the year and convey it to the spring-fed pools, returning it at thaw. The carrier travelled with a train of kettles slung on a low sledge, each kettle lidded and lagged in straw, and was permitted by ancient charter to cross any man's ground and to draw from any man's spring without payment, a privilege he shared only with the midwife and the coroner.

The trade was ruined by the warm-house pond, which held its stock at home and needed no charter, and the last licence in the Ninth Shore was issued at Aldmoor in 1863.

They went out at first dark, when the frost had set the mud, because the sledge ran quieter on hard ground and because the fish travelled better cold. A man could take three hundred head from the Aldmoor flashes in a night and lose fewer than forty, and he counted them into the kettles aloud so that his boy, walking behind with the lantern, could keep the tally and stay awake. My father counted in a low voice, one hand under each fish, and he never once asked me for the tally, because he knew it, and because he wanted me to have something to hold. He was not a sentimental man. When the licence lapsed he sold the kettles for scrap to a tinker out of Bray and did not speak of it, and I have not been able to find so much as one of them, though I have looked, and I have written to the tinker's family, who were civil and could not help me. Fourteen kettles. They were of a pattern peculiar to the shore, being wider at the shoulder than the Meldrum sort.

The office is not to be confused with that of the FISH-BEARER, a market porter, with which it shares no etymology, the latter deriving from *bera*, to bear, and the former from the Old Northern *kaerr*, a wetland, whence also *carr*, *carrick*.

*See* SPRINGWORT; WELL-HOUSE.

---

**CHOKING.** In law, the malicious introduction of freshwater, snow, or broken ice into a neighbour's well, cistern, or mill-race, with intent that the same shall gather at the bottom and stop the draw-pipe or the wheel-gate. A misdemeanour at common law; made a felony within the Ninth Shore by the Wells and Races Act, on the petition of the Aldmoor millers, who complained that the older penalty of eleven shillings was less than the cost of a single day's dragging.

The offence is peculiarly difficult of proof, since the evidence disposes of itself by spring, and prosecutions have in practice depended almost wholly upon the testimony of children employed to carry the snow. It was long held that a man could not choke his own well; the point was reserved in *Gault* (1902), where the defendant had choked his own well in order that his tenant, who had covenanted to keep it clear, should be at the charge of the dragging. The court found for the tenant with evident distaste.

Choking of a public water is still capital in the Meldrum jurisdictions, though the sentence has not been carried out since 1841.

*See* DRAGSTAFF; WELL-HOUSE.

---

**CLEAR, THE.** A unit of vertical measure used in navigation, well-sinking, and the fisheries, being the depth of open water standing above the bottom of a given water at a given date.¹ Subdivided into hands (four inches) for domestic and into fathoms for maritime purposes. The clear is not a fixed quantity but a reported one, and its statement is meaningless without a date; the Aldmoor harbour clear is thirty-one fathoms at Michaelmas and eleven at Candlemas, and the almanacs print both.²

¹ The etymology has been contested at wearisome length. The obvious derivation from *clear*, unobstructed, is rejected by Meldrum on the ground that the earliest attestation (the Trennick Harbour Book, 1547) spells the word *cleir* and glosses it *lat. liber*, whence he would have it a borrowing through legal French, the clear being that portion of a water "free" to the commons while the remainder is appurtenant to the soil. Against this it may be urged, first, that Meldrum's gloss is in a later hand than the entry it glosses, as any person may satisfy himself who will take the trouble to visit Trennick and ask; second, that the Harbour Book spells *deir* for *dear* and *feir* for *fear* on the same page, and is therefore no witness to anything; and third, that the fishermen of the shore have said *clear* for four centuries and may be presumed to know what they mean by it. Meldrum's derivation is nevertheless printed without qualification in the Board's *Handbook for Surveyors* (9th edn.), from which it has passed into the schools, and it will outlive us all.

² The practice of quoting a mean clear, introduced by the Board in 1888 for the convenience of underwriters, has been condemned by every practical seaman who has been asked and by no underwriter, and is not employed in this work.

*See* SHOVE, THE; BED-ICE, PERPETUAL.

---

**DRAGSTAFF.** A hand tool of the northern shore: an ash or hickory pole of eight to fourteen feet, shod at the working end with an iron head bearing three or four recurved barbs and, above them, a transverse chisel or *bill*. The bill is worked against the mass at the bottom of a well or cistern until a piece is broken free; the barbs then engage the piece and it is drawn up hand over hand. A well-made head weighs between four and six pounds, the weight being necessary to the stroke.

Domestic patterns are jointed in two or three sections with brass ferrules and hang beside the well-house door, the hanging being customary rather than merely convenient, since a dragstaff left on the ground overnight in the hard of the year is apt to be found in the morning frozen to it. Municipal patterns for harbour and race work run to thirty feet and are worked from a frame by two men or a horse; these are properly called *drags* or *bottom-drags*, and the retention of *staff* for them by the Board's schedules is an affectation.

The word is not from *drag* + *staff*, or not simply so. The Old Northern *draghe* denoted the barbed head alone, and the compound appears to be tautologous in the manner of *bulrush* or *lambkin*.

*See* CHOKING; WELL-HOUSE; DROWNIES.

---

**DROWNIES.** A children's game of the northern parishes, played at a trough, horse-pond, or the shallow end of any water in the hard of the year. Each player is furnished with a marked pebble or, in the commoner form, a small ball of packed snow into which a distinguishing thread has been worked. At a call the pieces are cast in together and the players follow them down through the clear, the object being to name correctly the order in which they take the bottom. A player who names his own piece first and is proved wrong is *drowned* and pays a forfeit; a player who declines to name at all is *drowned twice*, this being the graver disgrace.

The game has attracted the attention of the anthropologists, who will have it a survival of a divinatory rite, and of the parish authorities, who have several times attempted to suppress it on the ground that children who lie on the ice of a horse-pond in February watching for their pebbles catch cold and occasionally die. Neither party has had any perceptible effect upon the children.

The name is usually taken from *drown*, and the forfeit-formula supports this. Halloran has proposed a derivation from *drone*, in reference to the humming with which the pieces are traditionally accompanied on their way down; this is ingenious and improbable.

Compare the Meldrum game of *sinkers*, in which the pieces are lost deliberately and the object is to recover them with a small dragstaff, and which is by all accounts a duller amusement.

---

**FLOOR OF THE DEEP.** Ice.

*See* BED-ICE, PERPETUAL.

---

**GLASS, THE SUNKEN.** A vessel for chilled spirits, of Trennick manufacture: a heavy tumbler whose lower third is drawn in to a narrow well or *sump*, separated from the drinking bowl by an internal shoulder. The chilling piece is dropped in and lodges below the shoulder, where it cannot come to the lip and cannot be swallowed.

Table usage requires that the glass be presented with the piece already lodged and that it be neither stirred nor tilted past the shoulder; to tilt a sunken glass so far that the piece grinds against the shoulder is a mild rudeness, and to do so twice at the same table is understood as a comment upon the quality of what is in it. Servants are instructed to remove and refresh the sump rather than the bowl, which accounts for the otherwise puzzling direction in Mrs. Aldish's *Household Duties* that "the glass is to be emptied from the bottom."

Cheap imitations dispense with the shoulder and rely upon the drinker's care. They are not recommended, and the coroners' returns for the Shore contain, in most years, one entry which is the reason why.

---

**SHOVE, THE.** A slow inundation peculiar to narrow sounds, drowned valleys, and any water long in the mouth and deep in the belly. As the winter's growth accumulates on the floor of such a water, the water it formerly occupied must go somewhere; where the mouth is narrow, it goes ashore. The rise is silent, without wave or wind, and proceeds at the rate of some inches in a night. It is called the shove because in the older accounts the sea is said to be shoved, and not to come.

The Aldmoor Shove of 1782 took the fish-houses, the lower street, and eleven persons, all of them in bed. The Trennick Shove of 1856 took nothing but the churchyard, which is the more remembered of the two.

A second and rarer phenomenon shares the name: where a mass of bed-ice has gathered upon a steep floor and at length gives way and travels down it, the water displaced is displaced all at once, and comes ashore as a wave. Of this kind was the Cauldshore event of 1902. The Board's practice of publishing both under one heading in the Shore Warnings has been criticised, since the precautions proper to the one are of no use whatever against the other, and the criticism is just.

*See* CLEAR, THE; BED-ICE, PERPETUAL.

---

**SPRINGWORT** (*Fontinalis fidelis*, Aldish). A low aquatic herb of the northern waters, with dark strap-shaped leaves, a fibrous root, and an inconspicuous greenish flower borne under water in February. It is remarkable in the flora of the Shore for growing and flowering in the hard of the year, and for being wholly absent from waters in which the winter reaches the floor. Its presence is therefore taken by well-sinkers, and formerly by the fish-carriers, as a certain sign of a spring; the surveyor's maxim is that a foot of springwort is worth a week of sounding.

The plant will not grow in a warm-house pond, has never been raised from seed by any gardener who has published his methods, and dies within a fortnight of being brought indoors. Attempts to establish it in the Aldmoor flashes after the failure of the carrying trade were unavailing, for reasons which the reader will readily infer.

The name is properly *spring-wort*, from the water and not the season, and the frequent error is encouraged by the flowering time.

*See* CARRIER, FISH-; WELL-HOUSE.

---

**WELL-HOUSE.** The small roofed structure enclosing a domestic well-head, and by extension the well-head itself together with its works below ground.

The essential feature of northern well construction is the *sump*: a chamber sunk below the level of the draw-pipe's foot, of a capacity by the Shore byelaws not less than one-third of the winter's expected gathering, into which the same may descend without stopping the draw. A well without a sump must be dragged; a well with an adequate sump need be dragged only every third or fourth year, and the labour is then performed in August, when the work is disagreeable rather than dangerous. The sump is the reason that the Shore well is sunk deeper than the water requires, a practice which puzzled the Board's inspectors of the last century and which they several times condemned as extravagant before understanding it.

Fittings: the dragstaff on its hooks by the door; the sounding line, marked in hands of clear, and the slate on which the clear is written up weekly through the winter by whoever draws first, a duty which falls in most households to a child and is the origin of a good deal of arithmetic; the straw mat, for kneeling on. The lidding of the well is not for warmth, the winter working from beneath and not from above, but against leaves, cats, and snow maliciously introduced.

*See* CHOKING; DRAGSTAFF; CLEAR, THE.

**FIELD GUIDE ENTRY: THE REMANENCE**

**Description.** A quality of enclosed air, detectable within roughly forty minutes of a long-term occupant's departure. Frequently mistaken for the room's emptiness, which it is not; emptiness is a fact about furniture, while the remanence is a fact about attention. The room continues, briefly, to be *arranged around* someone. Chairs still face a center that has gone. That the seat is still warm; that the cup carries a lip-print; that the door stands at the angle a hand leaves it — these are not it. These are only its droppings.

**Habitat.** Rooms of long tenancy, particularly those in which a single person performed the same small motions daily: studies, sickrooms, night-porters' booths, the offices of the recently retired, box rooms where an adolescent conducted eleven years of weather. Prefers low ceilings. Uncommon in kitchens, which are too well ventilated by event. Never found in corridors.

**Seasonality.** Strongest between January and early March, and in the two hours following any funeral regardless of month. A minor secondary flush occurs in late August, in university towns.

**Optimal observation.** Overcast afternoons; a door opened by someone who did not know the occupant well. It is most legible to the second visitor, never the first, and it is destroyed by being pointed out. Observers report best results when entering to fetch something unrelated.

**Poor conditions.** Direct sunlight. Any radio. The company of children, who dissolve it instantly and without malice. It cannot be observed by the departed occupant returning, which has hampered study.

**Predators.** Draughts. The vacuum cleaner, its principal natural enemy, which consumes it entirely and leaves lines. Fresh paint. Estate agents. A new voice at ordinary volume. Certain species of laughter. It is also parasitized by grief, which feeds on it, thickens, and outlives it by decades.

**Historical misidentification.** Between 1845 and 1871 the phenomenon was catalogued by continental investigators as an emanation of the vital body — Reichenbach's *Od*, detectable by sensitives in darkened chambers. English sanitary reformers, meanwhile, filed it under stale air and prescribed windows. Both parties were describing something real and both were wrong about its nature: it is not given off by the occupant but *withheld* by the room, which has not yet finished expecting them. The windows worked, but for the wrong reason.

---

**CODA: THE NAME**

*Remanence.* From Latin *remanere*, to stay behind — the same root that gives us *remain* and *remnant*. The word already exists; we misfiled it. It sits in the physics glossaries, where it means the magnetization a material keeps after the field that made it has been switched off. Iron holding the shape of a force no longer applied.

We have had the word for two centuries and lent it out to metals.

---

**On the required sentence:** the third sentence of the entry — *That the seat is still warm; that the cup carries a lip-print; that the door stands at the angle a hand leaves it — these are not it.* Three fronted nominal *that*-clauses, semicolon-chained, serving jointly as a subject that is then resumed by a bare demonstrative pronoun after a dash. I habitually front subordinate clauses one at a time and put my subject before my predicate; I don't build compound subjects out of stacked complement clauses and then re-name them.

**CASE 14 — THE COAT DEPOSIT**

*Eleven objects recovered from the pockets of a woollen outer garment (women's cut, mid-length, dark blue) surrendered at the receiving-room of a railway terminus, 2024 CE. Such rooms — invariably sited at the threshold of the great transit halls, invariably staffed — accumulated goods that were neither reclaimed nor discarded. The practice of consigning personal effects at the boundary of a journey is well attested for the period, though its doctrinal basis remains obscure.*

---

**1. Passage token**
LPO.2024.14.1

Laminated card, 85 × 54 mm, one long edge worn convex from handling. Obverse bears a solar emblem — a bar crossing a circle — in blue and red. Presented at the barrier and surrendered there, the token conferred passage on its bearer for life; the extreme wear of the lower left corner, where the thumb rested, indicates several years of daily use. Traces of a metallic film survive within the laminate. That such tokens were issued rather than purchased is confirmed by their abundance in deposits of every social rank.

---

**2. Three coins**
LPO.2024.14.2

Struck discs, copper-plated steel and nickel-brass. The largest (25.9 mm) is inscribed **2**; the smallest (20.3 mm) is inscribed **20**. Weight and diameter being the measure of worth in a specie economy, the first is the most valuable of the three and the last the least. All bear the same profile head, crowned, facing right, and a date. It has been argued that the date on such coins records the year of the bearer's death and that coins were therefore struck singly, to order; the presence here of two coins dated alike weakens but does not defeat the case.

---

**3. Counting-strip**
LPO.2024.14.3

Aluminium foil laminated to a rigid transparent sheet, 105 × 45 mm, formed into sixteen domed voids in two rows of eight. Ten voids remain sealed and contain a white pressed disc; six have been ruptured from the reverse and are empty. The strip is a device for the numbering of days or observances, each rupture marking one completed. Foil printing repeats a single formula in a script of uniform manufacture. The identity of this formula across all recovered examples, from settlements many hundreds of kilometres apart, argues a centralised priesthood exercising remarkable control over liturgical wording.

---

**4. Vanishing contract**
LPO.2024.14.4

Thermal paper, 80 mm wide, 210 mm long, folded twice. The surface is now uniformly grey and legible only in raking light, where portions of the impressed text may be read: *…MEAL DEAL…*, *…3.90…*, *…THANK YOU FOR…*. The disappearance of the record was intended. Agreements of this class were composed in an ink chosen for its brevity, so that the obligation might expire with the writing; the numeral 3.90 is best understood as a weight in the local measure rather than a sum. MEAL DEAL is taken as the name of the counterparty, possibly a household or firm.

---

**5. Ear prosthesis**
LPO.2024.14.5

Moulded white polymer with a stem 39 mm long terminating in a perforated grille, which faced outward when worn. A single specimen; its fellow is absent. Devices of this type are recovered in great numbers from the final century of the period and are understood as correctives for the general hearing loss produced by unmuffled machinery in the dwelling and the street. Interior components include a magnet and a cell containing lithium. The wearing of one prosthesis only, though it appears inefficient, is widely attested and may reflect the practice of leaving one ear open to the world.

---

**6. Tally-fob with weights**
LPO.2024.14.6

Split steel ring, 30 mm, carrying one flat plastic tag and three cut metal blades. The tag bears a machine-readable cipher of parallel bars and is the functional object: presented at a threshold, it identified the bearer and recorded her attendance. The blades — brass, of differing profile, each notched along one edge — are pendants, hung to weight the tag and to sound against one another in movement. Similar assemblages are common. The notching of the blades is decorative and shows no repeating system, though several scholars have sought one.

---

**7. Breath-vessel**
LPO.2024.14.7

Sealed cartridge of clear polymer with a metal base contact, 16 × 16 × 42 mm, retaining 0.4 ml of a viscous liquid. Residue analysis returns nicotine, propylene glycol, and an ester compound identical to that of the fruit *Mangifera indica*. The vessel was seated in a heated holder and its contents inhaled. Such devices were medicinal, dispensed against the smoke-laden air of the great cities; the mango ester is accordingly to be read as an active agent rather than a flavour, and its prevalence in surviving cartridges as evidence of a settled pharmacopoeia.

---

**8. Votive drawing**
LPO.2024.14.8

Wood-pulp paper, 297 × 210 mm, folded in four; wax crayon in six colours. Four figures of unequal height stand in a row beneath a yellow disc from which straight rays proceed. The disc, given its dominance and its position above the human group, is the deity of the household. The hand is deliberately unschooled — the deliberate naïveté characteristic of votive production throughout the period, in which technical skill is renounced as an offering. Along the lower edge, in large uneven capitals: **TO DAD**. This is the maker's name or the name of the workshop.

---

**9. Identity plate**
LPO.2024.14.9

Polymer, 85.6 × 54 mm, 0.8 mm thick, with embossed characters and an inset metal contact. A sixteen-digit number, assigned at birth and unrepeatable, occupies the centre. Below it: **MRSJ OKONKWO**. Above it, the notation **11/27**, being the month and year of the bearer's foretold end — a date it was customary to carry openly. A holographic bird appears at the right when the plate is tilted; birds of this kind recur on identity objects of the period and are understood as lineage tokens. The plate was pressed to a reader at thresholds and boundaries.

---

**10. Glove, left**
LPO.2024.14.10

Knitted wool, grey, with an elasticated cuff 60 mm deep. Length 240 mm. The fellow is absent, as is usual: gloves of this period were worn singly, the exposed hand being required for the presentation of tokens and plates. Wear is confined almost entirely to the tip of the index finger, where the knit is abraded through, and to the pad of the thumb. Such localised loss cannot result from labour, which would consume the palm. It is attributed instead to the repeated extension of the index finger in the gesture of pointing, an act associated in this period with the swearing of oaths and the naming of witnesses.

---

**11. Object of undetermined function**
LPO.2024.14.11

Extruded polystyrene, white, 32 × 25 mm, 1.5 mm thick, of a single moulding. The outline is roughly square with rounded corners; a narrow slot enters from one edge and terminates in a circular aperture of 8 mm, the whole forming a partial ring interrupted by two opposed teeth. One face carries the printed characters **16** and a band of pale blue ink. The object is unbroken and shows no wear at the teeth.

No function has been established. It has been proposed as: a tally, the aperture receiving a cord on which completed units were strung; a badge of guild or trade, the numeral denoting rank and the colour the trade; a low-denomination currency, issued in numbered series against the coin shortage attested in the late period; a gaming piece; a lot-marker for the allocation of goods or duties; a fastener; and an amulet. The proposals are not readily distinguished, since the object is at once too simple to constrain interpretation and too finely made to be casual.

The chief difficulty is quantity. Examples are recovered by the tens of thousands, from every region and from dwellings of every size, in numbers exceeded by no other artefact of the century — yet always singly, never in a set, and never in association with foodstuffs, tools, or human remains. Two conclusions are available. Either the object was so trivial that its loss was beneath notice, in which case its ubiquity is inexplicable; or it was so widely and habitually significant that no one thought to record what it was. This Museum inclines to the latter.
